text:
静态逆了一遍 Claude，发现100台Mac Mini都救不了的八大天坑：

1. 手机插国区 SIM 卡：Sift 会记录下来，和出口 IP 国家对不上，直接完蛋

2. 清 App 数据换新号：基本没用，Sift 的 installation_id 就是 ANDROID_ID，硬件级绑定，服务端仍能判断

3. CLI 多账号共用 ~/.claude.json：device_id 不变、account_uuid 变，赤裸裸的一机多号

4. 桌面切号只换账号不换 userData：ant-did 特征会跟着，如果整包复制到新机等于把识别信息原样搬过去

5. 只给 https://t.co/JQehsPfVZy 配住宅IP：Sentry / Datadog / Sift / Segment 走机场，同一账号两条 IP 轨迹

6. 注册/支付/KYC：Turnstile、hCaptcha、Stripe 3DS、Persona 都会看提交那一刻的 IP

7. 已被限制的情况下换着 IP 反复请求：每请求一次，风控分数继续叠加

8. 一个住宅 IP 挂多个账号：明显的集群信号

author: markjeffrey
quoted_text:
1% of companies represent 90% of AI spending. 

Of that 90%, 80% of this spend are from unprofitable VC backed companies. 

So, roughly, $0.70-75 of every dollar of AI spending right now comes from AI companies spending VC investment dollars. 

As a result, the revenue quality in AI is currently poor. This happened in previous cycles as well, like cloud when early users of AWS were mostly venture backed startups. 

The thing, though, is that before AWS could scale and pull thru GCP and others as legitimate cash machines, there were a few clearing events to sort out these brittle revenues. 

This is the extrapolation of Ken’s point. We will need to transition from speculative AI spending to consistent, reliable spend that shows up in public market earnings reports. 

This hasn’t happened yet because most of the breathtaking revenue growth comes from LPs investing in VC funds who then send it to startups.

author: D2_Finance
quoted_text:
Jez read Reminiscences of a Stock Operator and shipped it on top Hyperliquid’ tech ( not @Lighter_xyz )

onchain bucket shop. he confirmed it in this thread under @dipsybitsy “yep, fully transparent and the losers who fund it will own.”

the bucket shop pattern is 100 years old. customer trades at the listed price, the house takes the other side, nothing reaches the actual exchange. 

Livermore made his early stake trading against them, then got banned from every shop in Boston for being too good. they died from two pressures: directional regimes that smoked the house, and ticker manipulation where operators pushed the real venue to harvest at the shop. both are live here. neither is solved by stacking five defensive parameters.

what is actually onchain: a contract that reads HL’s BBO via precompile and synthesises swaps against a Martingaler LP. zero flow reaches HL’s orderbook. zero funding rebalance. the only feedback loop is parasitic. 

BBO manipulation attempts to harvest the synthetic spread degrade HL’s book without compensating the makers wearing the jitter. the venue extracts liquidity quality from @HyperliquidX ( fair enough!)

the fair launch plus 1000x leverage plus PAPER mint-on-loss design is engineered for initial FOMO. expect a fast first week/month. Jez’ inner circle volume comes in, asymmetric impact taxes the few winners, losers fund the LP and mint PAPER, the chart can look initially great if execute right. 

this is the bootstrap window the docs explicitly subsidise at 100 PAPER per $1 of LP gain below 2M.

Then path dependence will shows up. 

LP edge per trade is thin: 0.2 bps jitter band plus the convex bite of asymmetric impact on winning closes. order of magnitude, on a $1M ticket the LP edge is in the tens to low hundreds of dollars. one 5% adverse move on $1M of net synthetic exposure is $50,000 of MTM loss. edge accrues like √t under stationary flow. directional regime hits the LP linearly in t. √t vs t means one persistent trend eats months of accrual. 

the half life of LP equity in a trending regime is short, and it gets shorter as size scales because the OI cap trails realised OI rather than leading it.

then the debt queue activates. 

martingaler issues claims paid by the next loser. once the queue is observable, the EV of opening a new position is negative twice: once because winners get haircut, once because withdrawals sit behind every prior bust. rational flow stops. Queue does not clear. 

PAPER, a claim on future LP revenue, is then a claim on revenue that must clear the queue first.

the cross-venue attack (@NaiveKrypto point in the thread) has its own path dependence. 

wicking HL spot or perp to harvest the synthetic at the shifted BBO is only EV-positive once papertrade’s OI is large enough that the harvest exceeds the cost of pushing HL. 

below that threshold, no one bothers. above it, every desk with an HL maker does. 

self-limiting at small scale, openly hostile at large scale. the steady state is zero, the only question is the path.

all bucket shops are zero in short to medium term. the 1900s wave died within two decades, mostly to regulation and to operators eating them. the onchain version skips regulation but keeps the operators and adds a debt queue that hard-codes path dependence into the equity curve. the docs read like a list of every defence shops historically tried, in order. 

stacking five does not change the shape of the failure mode, it just shifts where the failure surfaces.
closing thought. the whole structure is short volatility against directional flow, dressed up as a perpetuals venue. 

it is the same trade as a Korean retail account systematically selling MRNA noise reversion while their own KOSPI 200 trends straight through the stop. works beautifully until the regime turns, then the half life is a week.

clever paper, novel emissions curve, real engineering. the structure is 100 years older than the precompile.

author: sreeramkannan
quoted_text:
A few reflections on the lattice vs. hash-only debate that our recent Aerie post sparked:

1. Cryptographic ossification for blockchains was never safe. Until the day we know with certainty that P ≠ NP, that finding short vectors in lattices is intractable, that Keccak effectively behaves like a random oracle in deployed SNARKs, and that every single bug has been eliminated from our codebases, blockchains cannot ossify. That is simply not how safe systems are built. Issues will arise, and the system will have to respond.

It’s a double standard to reject lattices because blockchains are hard to upgrade if lattices break, while counting on upgrades if AI breaks your hash function or finds a critical zkVM bug.

The best counterargument is that hash-only designs are more agile: if your hash function breaks, just swap out the hash. But we must aspire to a higher level of agility than this. Indeed, as I cover next, if SNARK recursion itself turns out to degrade security, the proposed hash-only blockchain designs would need to be rethought from the ground up.

2. The real security debate is not lattices vs. hashes — it is lattices vs. building everything on SNARK recursion. That’s because “hash-only” is not really hash-only: it rests on hashes plus the soundness of deep SNARK recursion. Ethereum’s roadmap relies on exactly that: hash-based aggregation needs recursion to keep up with a slot’s worth of signatures, and EIP-8288 would send other signature schemes and users’ own proofs through the same recursive pipeline. In contrast, Aerie proves a slot’s worth of signatures on one laptop without any recursion.

All deployed post-quantum SNARKs rely on the Random Oracle Methodology (via Fiat–Shamir) to establish their security. This is an idealization we know fails in the real world: we have explicit counterexamples where “SNARKs” coming out of this methodology are totally insecure when instantiated with any concrete hash function.

We generally ignore these counterexamples in part because they only arise when proving contrived, self-referential statements about the very hash function used by the SNARK verifier.

But proving statements about the verifier’s own hash function is the exact thing you do in SNARK recursion. That’s why the security of recursive SNARKs can’t be established even in the random oracle model.

On top of that, the standard security proofs for recursion (in other models) suffer an “extractor runtime” blowup that is exponential in the recursion depth, suggesting that security may degrade as more recursion is applied. Yet Ethereum’s own EIP-8288 enables unlimited-depth recursion, even as it lists soundness of recursive SNARKs as a trust assumption. Proofs in more idealized models avoid the blowup, but they mainly tell us that an attack on SNARK recursion would have to exploit the concrete hash function, which is exactly what the Fiat–Shamir attacks above do.

To be clear, we don’t know of any outright attacks on SNARK recursion, and I very much hope it is secure. But some of us who have studied the question have a lingering sense that an attack may be possible in some settings. And if AI is going to supercharge cryptanalysis, there is no reason to expect it to spare Fiat–Shamir for SNARKs, let alone SNARK recursion, both of which have had far less scrutiny than lattices.

So, I do not concede that a “recursion everywhere” hash-only approach is clearly more conservative than one built on standard lattice assumptions.

3. “Just wrap everything in a hash-based SNARK” (like EIP-8288) faces challenges.

Aggregating signatures and proofs off-chain into a single block-level proof is a powerful design independent of the hash-only vs. lattice debate, and I am not telling people to avoid it. But claiming, as Vitalik Buterin did this week, that users can run whatever cryptography they want locally and wrap it in a client-side leanVM proof glosses over major hurdles.
For example, leanVM today is a minimal VM designed almost entirely to prove hash-based signatures and recursion, not general-purpose computation. And binary-field SNARKs like leanVM remain slow at proving the integer multiplications that lattice cryptography does en masse.

I am optimistic that many of these zkVM challenges can be met (including via my own work, binary-field Twist and Shout, which are now implemented in Magnetar). But regardless, if lattices can make aggregation simpler and faster, then they should be leveraged. We need to be agile no matter what.

4. For chains whose reason for existence is privacy, I truly struggle to understand the pushback. Public-key encryption (and fast single-server PIR) cannot be built from hashes alone, at least not in any black-box way. If lattices break, it is going to be very, very hard for these chains to provide acceptable levels of privacy and functionality. For a project whose entire reason for existence is privacy, a loss of confidentiality is an existential failure. Next to that, a second signature upgrade (after the first one, from elliptic curves alone to, hopefully, a hybrid lattice scheme) is easy.

Summary: We don’t know for sure what is secure and what isn’t. We are all weighing unquantifiable risks against each other, and we do not need to agree on a total order on them. But hash-only solutions face many open engineering challenges, and they are not more “conservative” in the way some have argued. Some of those challenges are entirely prosaic and have nothing to do with bugs or cryptography, like hardware support for custom schemes whose hash function is still undecided. I hope we can overcome those challenges within the appropriate timelines, but they must be acknowledged and portrayed realistically.

Overall, cryptographic agility and defense in depth (e.g., hybrid signatures) are the answer, which is why we are building both lattice-Jolt and hash-Jolt. In practice, the positions are less polarized than social media discourse suggests: for example, StarkWare is working to make Falcon verification cheap (https://t.co/FM68hmkqRx), which is great to see.

Here is the (apparently) controversial take I am sticking to: Conditioned on agility, whenever lattices make systems simpler or more functional, we should embrace them rather than default to “hash-only” designs. Lattices are what the rest of the world will depend on, with decades of study and hardening behind them, and at the system level, less functional often means less secure. Where hash-only designs are just as simple and functional, by all means use them.

text:
很喜欢用 DNA 双螺旋做比喻。

第一条双螺旋是资产和技术。

很长一段时间里，加密行业没有基本面。如果说有，那就是 BTC 作为电子黄金的共识。几乎所有资产都和 BTC 高度相关，本质上都是 BTC 的 beta。

这会带来一个很「悖论」的结果：价格本身就是基本面。资产就是价格，价格就是资产。

会给股票投资者，尤其是价值投资的拥护者，带来巨大的认知失调。BTC 越涨，加密行业越发展，他们就越无法理解。当然，如果思路打开一些，「稀缺」其实是一种更简洁、更接近经济学原理的「价值」。

关于技术，整个行业一直在发生基于区块链的原生创新（感谢 EVM）。只是在没有基本面支撑的情况下，资产价格总是垄断了注意力和话题。

第二条双螺旋是交易所和公链。

前者有最好的商业模式，可以穿越周期。后者是创新发生的温床。

之前，这两条双螺旋都是解耦的，各干各的。

直到 Hyperliquid。

它第一次同时让「资产价格 vs. 技术」和「交易所商业模式 vs. 公链」都 make sense。

这是一个新物种：一个金融科技区块链基建，用公司的逻辑在运转。有收入，代币有回购，有健康的商业模式。同时，它也在定义下一代金融应该建立在什么样的区块链技术之上。

这会继续带来认知失调，也会让人不适应。

但这只是开始，很多东西都会变。

这是一个好的开始。

text:
下午和一位老朋友聊天。其实我们现在都不怎么关注加密行业了，只是偶然聊起了一件挺有意思的事。

十多年前，我们最初都是被「去中心化」的精神吸引进这个行业的。

那时候真的有一种赛博乌托邦的浪漫感。觉得这件事很 Cool，它不仅代表着某种技术上的进步，也象征着一种精神上的独立，一种与传统强权主义割席的姿态。

但这么多年过去，我们都不再那么想了。

至少对我而言，这十多年的从业经历让我逐渐意识到一件事：

如果只有漂亮的口号，却没有具体的规则、制度和责任约束，那么所谓的自由，最终几乎不可避免地会滑向毫无道德底线的混乱。

更讽刺的是，当一些人高喊「去中心化」时，他们想表达的似乎早已不是创造一个更透明、更公平、更有社会价值的系统，而是另一句潜台词：我不需要对任何人负责。

行业发展了十几年，如果今天还指望这群人凭借自律，主动建立更透明、公平的行业标准和制度，我觉得多少有些自欺欺人。

因为不管是我自己亲身经历的，还是耳闻的信息，很多所谓的大佬哪怕第一桶金来得并不光彩，在获取巨额财富之后，似乎也从未想过让自己变得光彩一些，更没有想过承担什么行业责任或社会责任。

反而颇有一种土老肥的乡村企业家的气质：有钱就是正义，有钱就代表成功，也不需要承担任何的行业责任感，也不需要创造任何社会价值。

有时候我也分不清，究竟是这个行业的属性塑造了这样一群人，还是这样一群人最终塑造了这个行业。

这也是我十多年来一个挺大的思想转变：

从最初相信去中心化、崇尚不受干预的自由，到如今反而支持这个行业接受更严格的外部监管。

就有点像叶文洁的心态。

靠这群人自己，大概是没救了。或许只能寄希望于某种更高层级的外部力量介入，重新建立规则与秩序。

至于这种介入最终会让一切变得更好，还是更坏？
谁知道呢。

Alright. @Citi just published a 24-page note on $AAVE, and I promise you this is a much bigger deal than it sounds.

One of the world's biggest banks is now covering DeFi's biggest, most successful project in earnest. Citi has nearly $3T in total assets. This is not something to ignore.

Aave has long been seen as a crypto lending app. Citi calls that framing "increasingly incomplete" and sees Aave as "in essence, a decentralized collateral mobility ecosystem"

Citi's summary: "Tokenization answers the question of how assets move onchain. Aave is attempting to answer the question of how those assets will be financed once they get there"

That means you can pledge a tokenized Treasury fund or stock, borrow dollars against it at any hour, and keep the position

Citi thinks collateral mobility "may ultimately prove to be one of tokenization's most important use cases," and the note puts securities financing and "potentially prime brokerage itself" in scope

That statement is beyond huge to hear coming from Citi.

For context, the US repo market alone averaged about $12.6T in daily exposures in Q3 2025 (Office of Financial Research)

Citi's own September report on tokenized collateral shows why banks care:

- The biggest banks manage about $74B of collateral a day across about 65 custody locations
- Inefficient collateral costs a top-tier firm about $346M a year
- 77% of institutions expect to use some form of tokenized collateral in 2026

The pitch is simply too good. I think they are going to use AAVE

Standard Chartered has been way ahead of Citi and everyone else on this. Geoff Kendrick started covering AAVE in June with a $3,500 target for the end of 2030, about 23x from here

When I asked Kendrick about Aave on @MilkRoadDaily on Oct 1, he said it "dominates essentially an on chain bank space," and that at its peak last year it would have ranked as about the 35th largest US bank

At $149, AAVE's market cap is $2.30B and the token is down 32% over the past year, which is still the result of the market pricing it like it's just a crypto lending app

The caveat is that it is still very early days on all of this. Tokenized stocks on Aave were $4.7M of $31.9B in deposits as of Oct 7th. Tiny, but tons of room to grow.

Revenue is still soft too, down to $18.0M in Q3 from $37.9M in Q1 (Aave dashboard), and buybacks have been paused since April.

The progress is undeniable, though. Aave's Horizon market already lends stablecoins against tokenized funds like Janus Henderson's JAAA and VanEck's VBILL. These proof-of-concept products are just the beginning IMO.

Tokenized assets only get useful once you can borrow against them. $2.30B is a small market cap for the lender best placed to write those loans

Full disclosure: $AAVE is a position in my Milk Road PRO portfolio. Our PRO team was early to $UNI (+54.8%), $AERO (+93.7%), and $SKY (+42.6%)

almost a year later, kinda wanna revisit this

the title reads like a direct counter to long degeneracy, but that's not really what i was going for - i may or may not have clickbaited. long degen is more of an investment thesis about owning casinos (which i agree with, s/o jez), while short degen is from a trader / gambler pov about knowing when to leave the table

i think it's fair to say gambling has been pretty -ev since the article. perps have gotten increasingly difficult and memecoins are becoming a more solved game with lower ceilings. there's been plenty of opportunities to compound wealth recently, but i haven't seen many newly minted gambling millionaires

the framing i was going for was more of a call to return to long-term games, whether that's building something or developing better trading habits, rather than trying to gamble your way to millions. the glory days of that are behind us sadly, at least until there's a net new game and we get another pumpfun or hyperliquid moment

definitely sucks, i enjoy nothing more than making a ton of money gambling in a new, inefficient market. still not really sure what the next game is or if we even get one. we've seen attempts at new games, but they've mostly been reframings of or things built on top of existing ones: stock pairs, 1000x lev, etc. cool things, but not quite the 0 -> 1 moment needed to create an entirely new game

guess going forward the focus continues to be on thesis-driven trading/investing until there's something new where you can turn your brain off and gamble. can probably still long existing casinos and do well. don't think shorting casinos is ever a great trade, given how reflexive they can be in risk-on conditions. think the best way to express short degeneracy is just practicing better habits and playing better, longer-term games. more or less, un-fry yourself

text:
Grok Bot summary: SpaceX Q3 2026 Earnings

- This is SpaceX's Q3 2026 earnings webcast, streamed live on X from the Starlink factory and future StarMine production site in Bastrop, Texas.
- The speakers were Andrea Williams (head of investor relations), Elon Musk, Gwynne Shotwell (President and COO) and Bret Johnsen (CFO), followed by questions from analysts and retail investors.

Headline numbers (Q3 2026 vs Q3 2025)
- Revenue was $14.6 billion, up 161% from $5.6 billion.
- Net income was $4.4 billion, compared with a net loss of $1.1 billion a year ago. That's a $5.5 billion swing.
- Adjusted EBITDA was $8.8 billion, up 306% from $2.2 billion, growing faster than revenue again.

Elon on Starship
- Flight 14 was a critical milestone. Starship reached orbit for the first time and deployed working Starlink V3 satellites.
- On Flight 15, expected next month, SpaceX will try to catch both the booster and the ship. If it works, it will be the first time an orbital rocket has been fully recovered.
- Elon called full reusability the only way to extend consciousness beyond Earth for the long term. Success on the first tries isn't guaranteed, but he thinks it's more likely than not. He expects a steady stream of flights through the end of the year and more next year.
- The new Louisiana spaceport could eventually have 20 or more launch towers and move millions of tons a year to orbit and beyond.
- Starship should fly weekly at some point in the first half of next year, and twice a week or more by the end of next year. Early flights will need some refurbishment, but the goal is to land and relaunch like an airplane.

Elon on Starlink
- Flight 14 deployed 26 terabits per second of Starlink bandwidth while only about half loaded. That equals 10 Falcon 9 launches.
- In about three years he expects roughly 100 times the bandwidth of today's network. That means around 100,000 satellites, each with more than 10 times the bandwidth of current ones.
- Starlink revenue should grow roughly in line with the bandwidth it delivers. Fast direct-to-cell service and ground networks are being added too.
- He expects demand for about 1,000 times more bandwidth in three to five years. AI agents will each use far more bandwidth than a person, and there will be far more of them than people.

Elon on SpaceX superintelligence
- The main limits on rolling out superintelligence are now power, cooling and infrastructure, more than chips.
- SpaceX carries almost 90% of all mass sent to orbit, versus about 6% for China and about 4% for the rest of the world, including other US companies. The same team is now building computing infrastructure on the ground. Elon compared it to "the New York Yankees playing in Little League."
- He has often been spending four days a week in Memphis getting the supercomputer clusters running.
- SpaceX is on track to bring about 200,000 GB300 chips online each month for the rest of this year. It plans to keep that pace next year, mostly with Vera Rubin chips. In the Q&A he put the current rate at 220,000 GB300s a month.
- His computing power targets:
  - About 2.5 to 3 gigawatts (GW) online by the end of this year.
  - He's fairly confident of an extra 10 GW in 2027, and would be surprised by anything under 13 GW total by the end of next year.
  - SpaceX is aiming to add 20 GW of power and cooling next year so that power isn't the bottleneck. That makes it small but possible that compute grows by more than 20 GW next year.
- The most powerful training cluster is planned for the end of Q2, with 440,000 Vera Rubin chips. Elon said it should make Grok extremely competitive, possibly the best model.

Elon on Grok Bot
- It's the fastest-growing product Elon has ever seen.
- The more people use it, the more they keep using it over time.
- It's in early rollout with trusted business customers. A wide business rollout is expected within a few weeks, so companies can use it in teams "as though it were a virtual human."
- He thinks Grok Bot may end up using most of SpaceX's superintelligence computing power.
- His bottom line: SpaceX's annual recurring revenue (ARR) at the end of 2027 could be "somewhere between 500 billion and a trillion" dollars. He joked he didn't want to give Bret a heart attack.

Gwynne on launches and space operations
- SpaceX had 35 launches in Q3:
  - 21 Starlink flights on Falcon 9
  - 2 Starship flights
  - 12 major customer missions, including a Falcon Heavy carrying NASA's Roman Space Telescope into deep space
  - 6 national security launches
- New business won:
  - Three more crewed Dragon missions, filling the schedule through 2028
  - The Starlink communications contract for NASA's Artemis 3
  - 18 new national security launches
  - A contract to land a payload on the Moon with Starship
  - Three new Starfall missions on Starship
- Starfall is SpaceX's capsule for regular, fairly low-cost research in zero gravity, such as cancer and diabetes studies. A Starfall mission flew on Falcon 9 the day of the call.
- On October 1, SpaceX flew three Falcon missions from its three Falcon pads in just 13 hours. They were Crew 13 to the space station, a Falcon Heavy mission for the National Reconnaissance Office, and a rideshare carrying 130 payloads.
- Starship goals:
  - Catch both stages at the tower this year
  - Refly the upper stage by early next year
  - Attempt refueling in orbit early next year
  - Start flying Mobile V2 and StarMine satellites in 2027
- After helpful talks with the FAA, SpaceX expects the Flight 15 license to allow both stages to return to the launch site and be caught by the tower.
- She called Starship's move to Louisiana "the second Louisiana purchase."

Gwynne on Starlink
- Starlink now operates in 174 countries and territories. Vietnam and Uganda were added this quarter.
- It added 1.6 million home customers in the quarter, reaching just under 14 million (Bret gave 13.6 million). That doesn't count hundreds of thousands of business and airline customers.
- It helped in 25 disasters in Q3, including the Venezuela earthquake, an earthquake in western Colombia and Hurricane Lowell in Hawaii. In Venezuela alone it donated more than 1,400 kits, connecting over 250,000 people.
- Airlines:
  - About 12,000 planes are under contract, almost a quarter of all eligible aircraft.
  - Starlink has deals with three of the four biggest US airlines.
  - Lufthansa, Swiss, Copa, Korean Air, Austrian and Asiana flew their first Starlink-equipped planes in Q3.
  - Production of aviation equipment has quadrupled since January and should double again by the end of the year.
  - Flights with Starlink tend to be fuller.
- Starshield, the government version of Starlink, keeps growing. Business revenue and government revenue are each on pace to pass home-customer revenue in the future.
- Starlink Mobile:
  - Service started with new phone carriers in Uganda, DR Congo, Kazakhstan and Costa Rica.
  - It passed 22 million monthly users, up 37% from last quarter.
  - The FCC approved launching 15,000 Mobile V2 satellites.
  - SpaceX agreed to buy a set of low-band airwaves, which it says opens the way to becoming a major US mobile carrier.
  - The plan is to launch the V2 satellites through next year and turn on service in early 2028.

Gwynne on the superintelligence business
- Grok Bot, the AI assistant that can take actions for you, launched in August. Earlier this month it reached 800,000 paying weekly users, more than doubling in a month.
- Businesses are its fastest-growing group of customers. They use it in sales, marketing, IT and engineering as an always-on teammate.
- New Grok models are coming out faster, with big performance jumps expected soon.
- Bringing in Cursor is going well and gives SpaceX a large business sales team.
- The number of Grok business customers spending more than $1 million a year, including Cursor's customers, rose 50% from last quarter on a combined basis.
- Last week SpaceX announced a single plan that bundles Grok, Grok Bot, Cursor and X Premium.

Bret on results by business
- Space:
  - Revenue was $1.8 billion, up 84% from last quarter and 6% from last year, helped by a good mix of customers.
  - Spending continues on Starship, Raptor engines and vehicle production, Gigabay construction, and several launch pads at Starbase and Cape Canaveral, plus the new Louisiana site.
- Connectivity:
  - Revenue was $5.2 billion, up 69% from last year and 22% from last quarter.
  - There are 13.6 million home customers, with 1.6 million added in Q3, mostly in wealthier countries.
  - Making more V5 kits eased the stock shortage. Kits went to stores ahead of the holidays, which should boost Q4 sign-ups.
  - Average revenue per home customer rose 5% from last quarter to $69 a month.
  - Business and government revenue grew 91% from last year and 18% from last quarter, driven by Starshield and airlines.
  - Gross profit doubled from last year. Gross margin was 55%, including a one-time boost of about 3 points, mostly from tariff refunds. Without one-time items, the adjusted EBITDA margin rose about 2 points from last year.
  - Each Starship launch is working toward carrying more than 20 times the download capacity of a Falcon 9 launch today. Mobile V2 satellites start flying on Starship from 2027.
- Superintelligence:
  - Revenue was $7.6 billion, up $5 billion from last quarter and $6.7 billion from last year. Most of that came from growing contracts to rent out computing power.
  - SpaceX ended Q3 with 1.7 GW of rated computing capacity, and more data halls came online in early October.
  - Revenue from AI products and infrastructure was $7 billion. Of that, $608 million came from Cursor, whose purchase closed around the middle of the quarter. Without Cursor, this line still grew 192% from last quarter.
  - New computing capacity is paying for itself in less than a year. Pricing is running slightly above the top of the $30 to $50 per watt range discussed last quarter.
  - Advertising revenue grew 19% from last year, helped by the new ad technology platform launched in Q2.
  - The segment's adjusted EBITDA was $5 billion, up $3.8 billion from last quarter and $5.4 billion from last year.
  - Operating income was $431 million, or $1.6 billion without $1.2 billion of Cursor-related stock pay.
  - Of Cursor's $60 billion equity value, $23 billion went to keeping key staff and replacing their stock awards. That cost will be spread over about three years.
- Company-wide:
  - Capital spending in Q3 was $19.6 billion, mostly on AI computing, Starship facilities and satellite production.
  - The order backlog was $63 billion as of September 30. Of that, $17.5 billion has already been paid in advance, and about $42 billion should be counted as revenue within a year.

Guidance
- SpaceX is on track for $100 billion in annual recurring revenue by the end of 2026, based on December revenue times 12.
- Rated computing capacity should reach nearly 2.2 GW by the end of October and 2.5 to 3 GW by the end of Q4, with sites in Memphis and Southaven.
- Q4 capital spending is now expected to be $35 to $40 billion.
- Q4 gross margin should be closer to Q2's level, because Q3 had one-time boosts and a favorable mix.
- New guidance for Q1 2027 is total revenue of $33 to $37 billion.
- Spending is focused on three areas: AI computing, Starship, and next-generation Starlink broadband and mobile. SpaceX says it will keep a strong investment-grade balance sheet.

Q&A on the chip factory
- These are internal targets, which Elon said could be well off:
  - A first working test chip (something like a memory chip) around May or June next year at the research factory in Austin
  - Mass production around Q3 2028 at the main Terafab site at Gibbons Creek, possibly Q3 or Q4 2028
- He thanked ASML and other suppliers for delivering equipment faster. He hinted at possible chipmaking breakthroughs but wouldn't share details.
- The goal is for Terafab to eventually make "a terawatt of super intelligence chips per year."

Q&A on power, cooling and funding (Doug Anmuth, J.P. Morgan)
- Close to 3 GW should be done in the next few months. Elon said SpaceX is turning on about 220,000 GB300s a month, and that pace will speed up.
- He has a plan to add 20 GW of power and cooling next year, about 23 GW total, but won't share details. He's highly confident of an extra 10 GW (13 GW total) and says 20 is difficult but not impossible.
- One advantage is that SpaceX casts its own turbine blades and vanes, using the casting skills it built for rocket engines. Suppliers say blades and vanes take 12 to 18 months longer than the rest of a turbine, so SpaceX can bring power online 12 to 18 months sooner.
- SpaceX is also using solar, wind and other power sources. It sees promise in factory-built, modular AI computing units with their own power and cooling, spread across the country.
- Bret on funding: SpaceX has an investment-grade credit rating and a strong balance sheet. It's talking with several groups of lenders and can partner with suppliers and customers. Because the computing equipment pays for itself quickly, it starts funding itself, and cash from operations comes first.

Q&A on a Tesla merger (Edison Yu, Deutsche Bank)
- At shareholders' request, SpaceX and Tesla have each set up special committees of independent board members. Elon has a conflict of interest, so he can't take part.
- He said it would be wrong to assume a merger will happen. The committees haven't agreed on terms, and there's no guarantee they will.
- Tesla would need approval from 50% of all its shares, not just the shares that vote, which he called a high bar.
- He thinks a merger would be a good idea, since the two companies share work on AI software, chip design, Terafab, robots, StarMine launches and connectivity.

Q&A on Starlink Mobile (Evercore analyst)
- Gwynne said 85% to 93% of people's connectivity runs over Wi-Fi.
- S-band airwaves should carry most mobile traffic. The 800 MHz low-band airwaves carry less but are critical for reaching inside buildings.
- Small radios could be added to existing Starlink homes, businesses and towers, building on the equipment already in place.
- Elon sees a clear path to several hundred billion dollars a year in connectivity revenue and suggested a separate, longer presentation on the plan.

Q&A on how computing power is split (Eric Sheridan, Goldman Sachs)
- The rough goal is half for SpaceX's own use and half rented to others. That could swing to 60/40 either way from month to month.
- SpaceX prefers short-term contracts close to current market prices over long-term deals. The bet is that computing power will become worth more per watt as AI models produce more useful work per watt. Even old H100 chips rent for more now than when they were new.
- Contracts are renewing at higher prices per watt. Every major cloud provider and dozens of smaller companies want SpaceX's computing power, and it could rent out its capacity several times over.
- When SpaceX tried to rent outside capacity for running AI models, providers had none at all. Elon compared it to the Monty Python cheese shop sketch.
- He said it's not impossible that computing equipment pays for itself in six months next year.

Q&A from retail investors
- V3 satellites: users will notice faster speeds once a few hundred V3 satellites are up, likely by the middle of next year.
- Starbase Louisiana: the internal goal is a first Starship launch there in 2028. Elon says 2029 is highly likely, with launches at full scale in 2029.

Key takeaways
- Q3 revenue was $14.6 billion (up 161%), net income was $4.4 billion (up from a $1.1 billion loss), and adjusted EBITDA was $8.8 billion (up 306%).
- Superintelligence is now the biggest business at $7.6 billion, ahead of Connectivity at $5.2 billion and Space at $1.8 billion.
- SpaceX expects Q1 2027 revenue of $33 to $37 billion. It's on track for $100 billion in annual recurring revenue by the end of 2026, and Elon floated $500 billion to $1 trillion by the end of 2027.
- Computing capacity was 1.7 GW at the end of Q3 and is heading to 2.5 to 3 GW by year end. Elon is highly confident of 13 GW by the end of 2027 and is aiming for more than 20 GW.
- Computing power is very profitable. It pays for itself in under a year, pricing is slightly above $30 to $50 per watt, and demand is bigger than SpaceX can supply.
- Starlink has 13.6 million home customers paying $69 a month on average, 22 million mobile users, about 12,000 planes under contract, and service in 174 countries and territories.
- Grok Bot is the fastest-growing product Elon has seen, with 800,000 paying weekly users, and a wide business rollout is weeks away.
- Flight 15 next month will try to catch both stages, and weekly Starship flights are targeted for the first half of 2027.
- Capital spending is rising sharply, from $19.6 billion in Q3 to $35 to $40 billion in Q4. The order backlog is $63 billion.
- A Tesla merger isn't certain. The committees haven't agreed on terms, and it would need approval from 50% of all Tesla shares.

quoted_text:
$QCOM v $ARM 

Some "leaks" from the closing in the bench trial today that expose how Arm is trying to screw Qualcomm on the v10 ALA (assuming my math is correct).

TL;DR:
- Qualcomm offered Arm $250 million cash upfront in late 2024 to lock in v10 and settle the Arm v Qualcomm lawsuit.
- Arm rejected it, demanding a 15x rate hike ($28.20 per chip) through 2033 and a 34.5x hike ($64.86 per chip) through 2040.
- On Qualcomm's leaked $220 Snapdragon 8 selling price, Arm is demanding a 13 to 30 percent cut of gross revenue just for the instruction set.

Remember, the actual financial rate models have been heavily guarded under seal throughout this trial. But during closing arguments today, the attorneys tried to keep things properly sealed but blurted out several numbers in open court that let us do the math and piece the entire picture together. 

To understand the scale of what Arm is asking for, you first have to understand what Qualcomm pays today under its 2013 architecture license. 

Qualcomm's mobile royalty is capped at $1.88 per chip. The contract formula sets a low penny rate up to four cores, and for anything above four cores it charges 1.25 percent of the chip selling price, but with an absolute ceiling of $150. 

1.25 percent of $150 equals $1.875, which rounds to the $1.88 cap. On an eight core Snapdragon phone processor, that works out to about 23 cents per core. 

Now look at what Arm is demanding for v10:

For the first period (2027 to 2033), General Dunn stated openly in court that Arm is demanding a 15x increase over what Qualcomm currently pays. 
$1.88 multiplied by 15 is $28.20 per chip. 

For the second period (2034 to 2040), Dunn cited Dr. Kennedy's calculations from his sealed testimony showing the rate explodes to 34.5x what Qualcomm pays today. 
$1.88 multiplied by 34.5 is $64.86 per chip. 

While Arm's lead counsel Gregg LoCascio was arguing to Judge Noreika that rates need to rise because modern smartphone processors are much more expensive than they were in 2013, he had a slip of the tongue and leaked Qualcomm's actual flagship selling price in open court: 

"Today it's 220, it's ten times what some of them were in 2013."

There is your official public confirmation that Qualcomm sells its flagship Snapdragon 8 processor for roughly $220. 

Now we can connect those rate increases to Qualcomm's $220 chip price and look at what that means as a percentage of gross chip revenue.

- What Qualcomm pays today:
$1.88 divided by $220 equals 0.85 percent of the chip selling price. 

- Under Arm's 15x offer (2027 to 2033):
$28.20 divided by $220 equals 12.8 percent of the entire chip price. 

- Under Arm's 34.5x offer (2034 to 2040):
$64.86 divided by $220 equals 29.5 percent of the entire chip price. 

To put that in perspective for silicon engineering, standard off the shelf implementation licenses for pre designed Arm Cortex cores run around 1.5 to 2.5 percent. 

For an architecture license, Qualcomm spends billions of dollars of its own R and D to design custom Oryon CPU cores from scratch and only uses Arm's instruction set. Yet Arm is demanding between 13 percent and nearly 30 percent of Qualcomm's gross chip revenue just for the instruction set. 

That explains why Dunn told Judge Noreika that Arm's mobile demand alone would require Qualcomm to pay more royalties for phone CPUs than all of Arm's licensees combined paid across all products last year. And that the rate would exceed the ASP on some of the products. 

To make matters even crazier, LoCascio also revealed that during settlement talks in late 2024 right before the first trial, Qualcomm actually offered to write Arm a massive check upfront.

For context, Qualcomm paid $40.25 million upfront for its entire 20 year agreement back in 2013. Nuvia paid even less as a startup with a discounted upfront fee. 

Qualcomm offered a quarter billion dollars in cash upfront just to lock in v10 and settle the Arm v Qualcomm lawsuit. Arm rejected it because SoftBank and Rene Haas did not want a lump sum payment. They wanted the uncapped, recurring royalties that let them tax nearly 30 percent of Qualcomm's phone chips to feed Arm's internal goal of hitting $10 billion in annual licensing revenue by 2031 and forclosing Qualcomm out of the market. 

To me is not good faith commercial negotiation, that is an attempt to kill off custom silicon and force everyone onto standard Arm designs. And helps explain why General Dunn kept saying the evidence Noreika required was already in the case.

text:
Once you sustain $5-10m net worth, you've made it. Almost. Rich enough to be comfortable, poor enough for one bad bet to send you back. Here's what actually changes at this tier, and how to get to $25m 👇

-Self-funding, barely. A 3% draw on $7.5m is $225k/yr pre-tax, ~$150k after. You can quit but probably shouldn't. Earned income is still the cheapest capital you'll ever get plus it’s more reliable. -Risk capacity is real but finite. A venture bet going to zero is a bad year. Size so the worst case costs you a year or two, not a tier demotion. -Borrow, carefully. SBLOCs work here, just at worse spreads than the private bank crowd gets. Keep LTV under 20% so a drawdown doesn’t become a margin call. -Skip the fancy structures. Estate exemption is $15m per person. You don't have an estate tax problem, you have an income tax problem. QSBS, solo 401k, tax-loss harvesting, no state tax residency or Puerto Rico if extreme/mobile. Boring, cheap, compounding. -Claude Max is 0.03% of your net worth. Fading the singularity at this tier is a choice.

How to get to the next tier: 👇
author: thenarrator
quoted_text:
Once you sustain above $25m net worth, a lot changes:
-Self-funding at a conservative withdrawal rate. A 3% draw is $750k/yr pre-tax, and still about $450k after 40% tax. You never have to sell illiquid/venture positions at the bottom.
-Risk capacity. Girthy or illiquid bets that could go to zero become sizing questions rather than survival questions
-Borrowing > selling. Securities-backed credit at private-bank spreads pays for life and new deals while gains stay deferred. If you hold until death, the basis step-up erases those gains ("buy, borrow, die")
-Structures that pay for themselves. PPLI, exchange funds, CRTs and dynasty trusts carry fixed setup and administration costs that are only worth it around this level
-afford Claude Max/ChatGPT Pro with no sweat. Not stuck being a Luddite fading the singularity for 4 straight years

Lmk if any other questions 👇

text:
1% of companies represent 90% of AI spending. 

Of that 90%, 80% of this spend are from unprofitable VC backed companies. 

So, roughly, $0.70-75 of every dollar of AI spending right now comes from AI companies spending VC investment dollars. 

As a result, the revenue quality in AI is currently poor. This happened in previous cycles as well, like cloud when early users of AWS were mostly venture backed startups. 

The thing, though, is that before AWS could scale and pull thru GCP and others as legitimate cash machines, there were a few clearing events to sort out these brittle revenues. 

This is the extrapolation of Ken’s point. We will need to transition from speculative AI spending to consistent, reliable spend that shows up in public market earnings reports. 

This hasn’t happened yet because most of the breathtaking revenue growth comes from LPs investing in VC funds who then send it to startups.

DeepInfer 今天发布了，简单读了下，基础架构是完全从 vllm 的基础长出来的（至少这样看游神没有骗我们），方法名如 add_request，核心控制面，Sequence BlockManager Scheduler，metadata 中的核心数据 block_table 都是 vllm 那套，控制面全 cpp 书写。

这样看 tokenspeed 还算是走对了，至少早早开始做 cpp 控制面。

之前可能觉得 cpp 和 rust 控制面太嘉豪，因为控制面应该保证易用和可扩展性，可见我见识浅薄，当时 cc 还没开始大规模普及，对这些刻意书写 fully rust runtime 的工作不屑一顾。当时现在 coding agent 太过强力，管你什么生命周期，智能指针，统统一把嗦，到头来只要审代码的人能看懂就行，状态机的设计，都不用过分详细。

又一次证明了大厂的基模，和 ds 这种级别公司的差异，量化系统容不得 bug，容不得过分浪费资金，他们必须做到极致，这个风格，一以贯之，大厂则更多事得过且过，实用主义，在 maas 这件事上确实不如他们，并且他们上下全链路联合设计出来的模型，能力也极强，性价比远超我等。

从 3fs 到 deepgemm deepselect megamoe deepep...，然后是 dspark csa，dsh，全链路协同设计，只有 ds 这种地方能做到。
梁圣，真正有理想的人，脱离了低级趣味的人，改变世界的人。

text:
The recent renovation of Hollywood's Cinerama Dome, The Village & Bruin theaters in Westwood reminds me of the courage my friend Ray Howell had renovating the Warner Grand Theatre in San Pedro in 1984.

It was truly a labor of love & he convinced me & a handful of other cinema-lovers to join him in this odyssey, including film collector Mike Schleiger who put together ALL the classic film bookings; Morgan--an artist & former usher at the Grauman's Chinese Theater (where we had all worked) who helped with the painting restoration; and a number of veteran Mann Theater maintenance & concession mechanics who VOLUNTEERED their time to get the place in shape for opening day. Jack O., who had done all our hand & footprint ceremonies at the Chinese told me, "After all Ray's done for us over the years, he just has to say the word, and we're there for him." Now that's some kinda loyalty, yes?  

My time there was spent as manager, projectionist, and "tech guy"--it was a chance to both learn more about & share my love of film.  

There are also people who just love the SHOWMANSHIP of presenting a film to an audience & Ray was one of them. The fact that the Warner still exists, is due in part to his perseverance, hard work & love of cinema. FYI: Adding the word "GRAND" to the theater name was Ray's idea. It was not part of the original branding by WB, but it smacks of the grandeur of motion picture palaces of yesteryear, which the art deco design invokes and what Ray hoped the WG would be for the community of San Pedro.  

Glad to have lent a hand in helping to keep the movie-going experience alive in the 21st Century. 🍿

🚨 LABOUR COUNCILLOR WALKS FREE FROM COURT AFTER POSSESSING THE WORST INDECENT IMAGES OF CHILDREN 

A Labour Councillor has been given a 12-month suspended sentence for possessing indecent images of children deemed category A considered the worst.

Tom Dewey a Labour Councillor for Hackney has avoided jail after admitting possessing indecent images of children.

Recorder Jonathan Ashley-Norman handed down a 12-month suspended sentence, he said: Your actions have had a devastating impact on your life and your closest family.”

He gave him credit for an early guilty plea
He also ordered devices to be forfeited, told Dewey to pay £500 costs and put him on a 10-year Sexual Harm Prevention Order, which will restrict his contact with children.

Thomas Dewey, who was elected as a Labour councillor for De Beauvoir ward, was arrested by detectives from the National Crime Agency who seized laptops and tablets at his home in Hertford Road in Hackney, just days before May’s local elections last year.

He had a “huge problem” with looking at indecent images of children from the internet for his own use, Wood Green Crown Court heard.

Described by party activists as “ambitious”, he had worked at Hackney Council for nearly two years as a support officer for the Mayor and Cabinet office and for a consultancy advising on planning.

He was the branch secretary for the De Beauvoir ward for Labour and had spent years campaigning for the party in Hackney.

Last month, the 36-year-old admitted a charge of making five category A indecent images of children, a further charge of making 41 category B indecent images, as well as making 203 category C indecent images of children. 

Images are graded with category A considered the worst.

Dewey, now of Hampshire, also admitted a charge of possessing 78 extreme pornographic images of children – an act which results, or is likely to result, in serious injury to a person  and having 1,523 prohibited images of children in his possession.

The maximum sentence for the most serious charge is five years, depending on the number of images.

Details of the images were not read out in court, but prosecutor Margia Mostafa said the content of the Category A images “are highly serious.”

The starting point for the first charge is two years in prison but the steps Dewey has taken, along with his early guilty plea and remorse saw that cut to 12 months, suspended for two years.

He received an additional six months for charge two, three months for charge three, six months for charge four, and six months for charge five, all suspended for two years and to run concurrently.

Dewey also has to do 150 hours’ community service and 40 days of a “rehabilitation activity”.
,two days before his arrest at home in Hackney where he was “the sole occupant.”

The NCA seized two laptops, two tablets and a hard drive and Dewey was arrested and cautioned at 7.03am.

They had identified four  “CyberTipline” reports which has user ID to a google drive and Dewey had uploaded indecent images of children to his personal account.

Dewey was elected as a Labour councillor for the first time in the May 2022 council elections and resigned days later, triggering a by-election last July.

Labour, which has a majority on the council, narrowly defeated the Green candidate in the by-election.

The charges have caused upset amongst Labour campaigners who were unaware of the arrest until this summer.

text:
最近，一些用户收到身份信息更新提示，会有疑问：我已经认证过，为什么还需要更新资料？甚至出现了一些不着边际的猜测。用户的担心，我们非常重视，也有责任把问题解释清楚。

一、为什么认证过，还需要再次核实身份？
身份信息需要定期核实和更新。证件到期、个人资料发生变化，或账户进入定期复核，都可能需要补充或更新信息。这是此前就有的账户管理流程，因此，已经完成认证的用户，也可能再次收到提示。此外，本轮更新仅涉及少数用户，收到更新提示也不代表账户出现异常。

二、这次信息更新是否和税收政策相关？
无关。本轮更新属于既有的账户管理流程，并非为网传的税务催缴而开展。KYC（了解你的客户）帮助平台核实用户身份、识别和防范洗钱等风险，是日常合规管理的一部分，不只在开户时进行，也需要持续核实和更新。各家合规平台都需要执行KYC的责任，也都需要认真保护用户个人信息。

三、是否存在“交出资料换取上市资格”的安排？
谣言。“交资料换上市”的说法不属实。定期核实和更新身份信息，是此前就有的流程，不是临时增加的要求。如果将KYC和上市做强行关联，那没有上市计划的平台是不是就不需要做KYC了？

我们也注意到，近期短时间内集中出现了一批内容高度相似的帖子。背后是否有人推动，我们不做判断。但无论帖子来自哪里，用户提出的具体问题，我们都会认真回答。

text:
A few reflections on the lattice vs. hash-only debate that our recent Aerie post sparked:

1. Cryptographic ossification for blockchains was never safe. Until the day we know with certainty that P ≠ NP, that finding short vectors in lattices is intractable, that Keccak effectively behaves like a random oracle in deployed SNARKs, and that every single bug has been eliminated from our codebases, blockchains cannot ossify. That is simply not how safe systems are built. Issues will arise, and the system will have to respond.

It’s a double standard to reject lattices because blockchains are hard to upgrade if lattices break, while counting on upgrades if AI breaks your hash function or finds a critical zkVM bug.

The best counterargument is that hash-only designs are more agile: if your hash function breaks, just swap out the hash. But we must aspire to a higher level of agility than this. Indeed, as I cover next, if SNARK recursion itself turns out to degrade security, the proposed hash-only blockchain designs would need to be rethought from the ground up.

2. The real security debate is not lattices vs. hashes — it is lattices vs. building everything on SNARK recursion. That’s because “hash-only” is not really hash-only: it rests on hashes plus the soundness of deep SNARK recursion. Ethereum’s roadmap relies on exactly that: hash-based aggregation needs recursion to keep up with a slot’s worth of signatures, and EIP-8288 would send other signature schemes and users’ own proofs through the same recursive pipeline. In contrast, Aerie proves a slot’s worth of signatures on one laptop without any recursion.

All deployed post-quantum SNARKs rely on the Random Oracle Methodology (via Fiat–Shamir) to establish their security. This is an idealization we know fails in the real world: we have explicit counterexamples where “SNARKs” coming out of this methodology are totally insecure when instantiated with any concrete hash function.

We generally ignore these counterexamples in part because they only arise when proving contrived, self-referential statements about the very hash function used by the SNARK verifier.

But proving statements about the verifier’s own hash function is the exact thing you do in SNARK recursion. That’s why the security of recursive SNARKs can’t be established even in the random oracle model.

On top of that, the standard security proofs for recursion (in other models) suffer an “extractor runtime” blowup that is exponential in the recursion depth, suggesting that security may degrade as more recursion is applied. Yet Ethereum’s own EIP-8288 enables unlimited-depth recursion, even as it lists soundness of recursive SNARKs as a trust assumption. Proofs in more idealized models avoid the blowup, but they mainly tell us that an attack on SNARK recursion would have to exploit the concrete hash function, which is exactly what the Fiat–Shamir attacks above do.

To be clear, we don’t know of any outright attacks on SNARK recursion, and I very much hope it is secure. But some of us who have studied the question have a lingering sense that an attack may be possible in some settings. And if AI is going to supercharge cryptanalysis, there is no reason to expect it to spare Fiat–Shamir for SNARKs, let alone SNARK recursion, both of which have had far less scrutiny than lattices.

So, I do not concede that a “recursion everywhere” hash-only approach is clearly more conservative than one built on standard lattice assumptions.

3. “Just wrap everything in a hash-based SNARK” (like EIP-8288) faces challenges.

Aggregating signatures and proofs off-chain into a single block-level proof is a powerful design independent of the hash-only vs. lattice debate, and I am not telling people to avoid it. But claiming, as Vitalik Buterin did this week, that users can run whatever cryptography they want locally and wrap it in a client-side leanVM proof glosses over major hurdles.
For example, leanVM today is a minimal VM designed almost entirely to prove hash-based signatures and recursion, not general-purpose computation. And binary-field SNARKs like leanVM remain slow at proving the integer multiplications that lattice cryptography does en masse.

I am optimistic that many of these zkVM challenges can be met (including via my own work, binary-field Twist and Shout, which are now implemented in Magnetar). But regardless, if lattices can make aggregation simpler and faster, then they should be leveraged. We need to be agile no matter what.

4. For chains whose reason for existence is privacy, I truly struggle to understand the pushback. Public-key encryption (and fast single-server PIR) cannot be built from hashes alone, at least not in any black-box way. If lattices break, it is going to be very, very hard for these chains to provide acceptable levels of privacy and functionality. For a project whose entire reason for existence is privacy, a loss of confidentiality is an existential failure. Next to that, a second signature upgrade (after the first one, from elliptic curves alone to, hopefully, a hybrid lattice scheme) is easy.

Summary: We don’t know for sure what is secure and what isn’t. We are all weighing unquantifiable risks against each other, and we do not need to agree on a total order on them. But hash-only solutions face many open engineering challenges, and they are not more “conservative” in the way some have argued. Some of those challenges are entirely prosaic and have nothing to do with bugs or cryptography, like hardware support for custom schemes whose hash function is still undecided. I hope we can overcome those challenges within the appropriate timelines, but they must be acknowledged and portrayed realistically.

Overall, cryptographic agility and defense in depth (e.g., hybrid signatures) are the answer, which is why we are building both lattice-Jolt and hash-Jolt. In practice, the positions are less polarized than social media discourse suggests: for example, StarkWare is working to make Falcon verification cheap (https://t.co/FM68hmkqRx), which is great to see.

Here is the (apparently) controversial take I am sticking to: Conditioned on agility, whenever lattices make systems simpler or more functional, we should embrace them rather than default to “hash-only” designs. Lattices are what the rest of the world will depend on, with decades of study and hardening behind them, and at the system level, less functional often means less secure. Where hash-only designs are just as simple and functional, by all means use them.

quoted_text:
Thank you for this, @_NathanCalvin. I appreciate and am a fan of the investigative work you’ve done on behalf of AI safety and believe your comments are coming from a constructive, honest place, and that it benefits the public to have people whose job is to scrutinize the actions of frontier AI companies. I think something would be wrong if companies of the size of Anthropic didn’t get harshly criticized basically every day; strong antibodies against corporate power are a healthy feature of a free society, and especially so when issues of the gravity of the one we’re facing are at play. I also do agree that some of the examples you cite were mistakes by Anthropic.

That said, I disagree with the thrust of your post. At the core, a good fraction of the things you criticize are consequences of Anthropic’s basic theory of change that we have held for many years. Our strategy has always been what I’ve called the “race to the top” — by showing how it’s possible to build the technology responsibly, we can raise the bar for the entire industry. The forces that drive the race to the top are hugely more effective if the company practicing them is at the frontier; that’s one lesson I’ve learned repeatedly. And looking at that strategy as a whole, I’m proud of our track record and stand by it.

I believe that if we take a list of things that Anthropic did in the past year that were pro-safety and commercially costly to us, they far outweigh the list you’ve made, while at the same time I also disagree with some of the items on your list. Here are some things Anthropic has done, in the same period you’ve cited (the last year), which were very costly to us commercially while having strong safety benefits:

1. We played a key role in SB53 (and other state laws), at a time when doing so was politically perilous to the company and AI regulation was very unpopular. We in fact argued for a stronger version of SB53 than was ultimately passed; there were a lot of stakeholders and we were not the limiting factor in the strength of the bill that was passed.

2. We have very strong biological safeguards on our models, because we’ve seen concerning results in bio uplift trials and even seen and blocked potential attempts to misuse our models for bioweapons (as seen in our threat intelligence report from a few weeks ago). This is a very serious threat that we want to have zero tolerance for. But having very low false negatives means having significant false positives (despite months of effort on our part to improve the classifiers), enough so that biologists joke about how restrictive our classifiers are, and competitors sometimes sell against us by touting their more permissive bio capabilities. This has been very painful to us in an area where we care a lot about supporting an ecosystem of Claude users (biomedical science; and it is particularly frustrating to me as a biologist), but it’s the right thing to do and we intend to keep doing it.

3. Similarly, we first had Mythos-class models in February but didn’t make them generally available until June (when we had stronger cyber safeguards in place). We only offered them to a limited set of partners in order to focus on cyberdefense. It would have been much more economically rational to simply release the model to everyone. We likely sacrificed a significant chunk of a several-month model lead. But because of this, many companies secured their cyber infrastructure before the deluge of widely available cyber-capable models. Of course there are ways it could have gone better or been run better, but this was what we were aiming to do.

4. I advocated forcefully and publicly, in my essay Policy on the AI Exponential in June of this year, for the government to have the power to block model releases. Back then this was still outside or maybe on the edge of the Overton window, though I understand the window has moved since then. We were attacked intensely for this.

5. I don’t want to re-ignite conflict, but the events of February 2026 are a strong example. It is clear that our public stance could have seriously damaged the company’s future.

6. We’ve continued to advocate for export controls on chips and chipmaking equipment to China, because we think it allows democracies to negotiate from a position of strength on AI safety agreements. We’ve done this despite problems it’s created for us with industry partners who hold very different views and on whom we are very dependent.

7. As far as I’m aware we were the first, and still only, frontier company to restrict the sale of AI services to PRC-controlled companies, including those operating through third countries (otherwise a major loophole). We’ve therefore forfeited significant short-term business to prevent fueling AI platforms and applications that would help the CCP’s military and intelligence services. We are also cracking down on distillation; generally, distillation is not a major threat to us commercially, but like chip exports it has concerning national security and safety implications, so we expend significant energy and company resources to address it.

8. As you mentioned, we’ve put out a lot of reports, announcements, long model cards, public advocacy, etc, all trying to inform the public about the risks of AI. These involve a level of detail and effort that would be implausible for a purely profit-maximizing company.

9. Just this week, we announced we were putting 5% (and possibly more over time) of the company into a public benefit fund.

All of these decisions came with very substantial costs to us. To be fair, those that involved holding back or restricting access to frontier capabilities also had a broader cost — for example, the public might otherwise have benefitted from faster progress in biology, so I am not saying that our decisions were without tradeoffs — but they were not driven by profit-seeking.

For each decision, you can come up with ulterior motives that could have driven us — I think it is a general truth that any decision, on any topic, can always be portrayed as a nefarious scheme. But most of those end up being pretty farfetched or don’t fully make sense if you actually examine them closely. For example, it is deeply implausible that it would be a shrewd business move to block a large swath of research biology in order to do the work ourselves and compete with our customers; we expect the benefit to the ecosystem to greatly exceed the work Anthropic does itself, and for the two to complement each other. It is not in Anthropic’s interest to be perceived as unfriendly to biologists. Our Life Sciences Verification Program, which gives vetted biology professionals access to our models, also refutes this idea. 

Of course, a different set of people will see this and make a different criticism: that Anthropic shouldn't be making decisions about who gets access to what in the first place. I agree, in the sense that ideally the government would be making these decisions, and that’s why we advocate for regulation. But for now we are forced to make them, and enabling bioterrorism isn’t a better option.

I think that even if I conceded every item in your list, I would happily hold up mine next to it; I don’t think it’s a close call. That is of course partly subjective and different things are important to different people. Maybe one way you could object is that several of the items above relate to AI misuse and not loss-of-control; if you think the latter is much more important than the former, that might change your calculus. But this is not Anthropic’s view — we view both as serious issues. You can also disagree with our decisions, as many have, but they are consistent.

But I also disagree with at least some of your list. Several items don’t represent a deviation from Anthropic’s strategy or values at all, once we postulate the “race to the top” strategy that requires being a frontier AI company. Your items 1-4 are all simply examples of what it means to compete at the frontier, and we stand by them, both in the sense that they are transparently ordinary things to do as part of that strategy, and that we stand by the strategy as a whole. 

To be fair, there are important questions worth confronting (and that we are confronting) about what to do when the AI-driven acceleration gets fast enough that it is hard for safety to keep up. We are nearing that point and that’s what’s driving some of our thinking about “pacing.” But 1-4 are actions taken before that point and should be perfectly expected based on Anthropic’s strategy as a company. Of course it is possible to disagree with that strategy, but that’s a more fundamental disagreement that you could have had any time over the last few years.

I agree we could have handled your items 7, 8, and 9 better. All fall into the category of “rhetoric or policy communication that wasn’t carefully written or resulting from fast-changing circumstances not propagating from one team to another fast enough.” This kind of thing happens a lot in large organizations (Anthropic is over 5,000 people), and doesn’t even necessarily represent a failure or mistake of any single person. I am of course the CEO, and I take responsibility. The volume of communication from Anthropic is enormous and if these are the worst examples, I think we’re frankly doing pretty well, though I will continue to work hard to make sure we do even better.

Your 5th item (the change to our RSP) is the most substantive item, and people can debate this, but I think that the old, more rigid RSP created a lot of situations where we were technically required to do something that required a lot of effort but in retrospect wasn’t very important for safety, as well as not covering some of the most important things. Our current RSP’s focus on transparency brought things like risk reports and roadmaps, and its emphasis on independent external review laid the groundwork for even more intensive embedded evaluation, all of which I think have been valuable in driving a race to the top. In the original announcement in September 2023, we described the RSP as an “early iteration that we [would] build on” and said that “rapid iteration…will almost certainly be necessary.” I understand that changing plans is always a move that creates justifiable scrutiny — I just don’t think we ever represented that we wouldn’t do so.

Relating to your 6th item (having an FCF in addition to our RSP), I know our intent is to meet the letter and spirit of our regulatory obligations (via our FCF) while also remaining able to experiment with more novel approaches to risk management that go beyond what the law currently requires (via our RSP). I promise to look into it further, as it’s a complex issue and it is possible we are not weighing the considerations in the right way.

Overall, although Anthropic has made plenty of mistakes as an organization — including some of the items on your list — I feel that we have repeatedly taken serious and substantive actions counter to our bottom line and that there is a significant negativity bias distorting assessments like the one you are making above. We’ll always try to do better but, again, I am extremely proud of our track record and stand by it. I will have more to say soon about how we are going to further live our values in this moment of rapid change.

text:
some thoughts. the current decode max for v4.1F+GB200 is 25.5K at 100 tps and 131K ctxt. 950DT with CANN, as per the Sep 30 benchmark, does 5K. At 230 tps: 20K vs 2.7K. From 5x to 7.4x. But: DeepInfer Nvidia uses EP64-128/DP64-128. 3 weeks ago, DeepSeek explicitly said in DeepEP-Ascend that they have not optimized EP64-128 (see pic 4, "Larger EP sizes and combine remain under optimization; combine has additional local reduction overhead and HBM contention with URMA. Huawei firmware improvements are also planned to reduce this contention") yet and they're working on it with Huawei. Today they recommend "ordinary 8-GPU machines for prefill, ordinary 64–128-GPU supernodes for decode". There is no 64-128 GPU "Nvidia supernodes". It may be they've solved that part at least internally, and that 100TPS case can improve to ≈8-10K in 128-Chip SuperNodes using DeepInfer with high EP.
(I ignore the actual mix for simplicity, directionally it'll be similar).
In that case, assuming $10M per NVL72 rack (reasonable current smuggling premium, extrapolated from >$1M per 8-GPU DGX B300 server a few months ago) thus $139K per GPU, and $37K per 950DT (rumored), Blackwells likely remain more economical in the actual V4.1F product regime, but clearly lose in the throughput-maximizing one (eg RL rollouts). The crossover is roughly 6.8K tokens/s/chip.
Given the efficiency of Blackwell inference and the competitive advantage of V4.1F being that fast (but still making a ton of dumb turns), it'd make sense for DeepSeek to cover the API with a small Blackwell cluster worth <$1B, ie ≈100 racks (it'll pay for itself in well under a year), and fully pivot to Ascend for post-training inference. They will do training of larger future models on Ascend SuperPoDs/SuperClusters, when available.

text:
很多人还没意识到 Codex 和 Work 这次搞的「永久缓存」到底意味着什么

目前绝大多数 API 的 Prompt Cache，生命周期基本卡在 12 小时以内。超过这个窗口，缓存自动失效，状态全部清空

但 Codex 和 Work 的做法直接跳出了纯 API 的逻辑：把缓存与登录用户深度绑定，做到跨会话、跨周期的永久保留

哪怕一个重型项目你放置了几天甚至几周，只要重新拉起旧对话，上下文依然能稳定命中

这东西最大的价值不在于省了多少毫秒的延迟，而在于重构了 Agent 的经济模型：

边际成本被直接按死：缓存命中的 Token 价格直接下探到正常输入的 1/20（降幅 95%）。

1. 长任务的冷启动成本归零：在几十万 Token 的工程级代码库里，反复交互最烧钱的从来不是新生成的内容，而是每次回车都必须重新过一遍全部历史上下文。

2. 订阅制 Agent 的生产力杠杆放大：同样的月度配额，以前跑几个长周期任务额度就见底，现在等同于把有效交互轮次拉高了一个数量级。

真的进步太快了

text:
Do you remember that scene from The Big Short where Michael Burry knows something is fundamentally changing in the financial system but the market keeps moving against him while his investors begin losing faith?

I think crypto has been going through something similar.

We tried to speed run into the future by manufacturing enough catalysts for speculators to speculate on so we could attract liquidity into a new asset class.

Builders created the illusion of accelerated adoption and speculators believed they were betting on that acceleration.

But the actual timeline of adoption was never in our control.

It needed global liquidity. It needed integration with the existing economy. It needed the same institutions we once wanted to replace to find economic reasons to participate.

And while we kept selling the future as something arriving tomorrow, speculators kept paying for that illusion.

Now the interesting part begins.

What if the infrastructure is finally becoming useful enough for real capital to enter without needing another speculative narrative?

What if the speed run we spent years pretending to achieve is actually beginning?

The tragedy is that many who believed in that future early have already been burnt enough to stop believing.

Sometimes being early to the future is just another way of being wrong about time.

text:
山雨欲来风满楼？

08 年次贷危机前夕，少数资金通过买入 CDS（信用违约互换）成功押注了房地产市场的崩盘。

当下，市场也正在将同样的金融工具用于对冲 AI 算力基建的债务风险。

简单来说，CDS 本质上是企业债务的违约保险。买方支付保费，若企业资金链断裂无法偿债，卖方全额赔付。

数据显示，资金正在密集买入科技公司的这种违约险。9 月份，与美股七大科技巨头债券挂钩的 CDS， 周均交易规模突破 90 亿美元，较 7 月水平激增逾 4 倍。

另外，今年美国企业 CDS 指数的总交易量已超过去年全年。

甲骨文的 5 年期 CDS 一度升至 343 个基点。SpaceX 的 CDS 从 6 月的 111 个基点快速拉升至 240 个基点以上。

更为激进的新兴云服务商 CoreWeave（就是最近股价大跌的那家 $CRWV），其 CDS 利差直接突破 1000 个基点，这在债券定价模型中已被视为面临实质性信用压力的困境区间。

今年以来，全球企业为 AI 相关基建的借款规模已超 4500 亿美元，达到去年同期的四倍。底层逻辑正从初期的自由现金流支撑，全面转向高杠杆的债务驱动。

所以本质上，搞 AI 太烧钱了，巨头们现在的玩法已经从“花自己的利润”，变成了“疯狂加杠杆借钱”。

那么市场也开始怀疑，大厂们砸进 AI 里的钱，到底能不能按期赚回来？

当多资产基金和老钱们排队买入CDS 时，意味着留给科技巨头们兑现利润的时间窗口，已经非常有限了。

text: Been obsessed with the stock market since I was a teenager. Have traded through the dotcom bubble, the financial crisis and just about every market mania since. But I’ve never seen anything like the skepticism surrounding AI. Not even close. Every time one bubble narrative falls apart a new one takes its place. Rumors become headlines. Misleading data goes viral. Claims that could be debunked with 5 minutes of research get repeated by major media outlets, influential investors and Wall Street analysts. It’s relentless and honestly pretty fascinating to watch. Of course there will be spectacular failures and massive wealth destruction along the way. That’s what happens during technological revolutions. But I’ve never witnessed this much effort to convince the world that something so transformative is actually one giant speculative bubble destined to take the entire economy down with it. I understand why AI scares people. What I find harder to understand is why so many investors seem to be rooting for it to fail.

text:
Simple parameter changes can materially improve a network’s tokenomics.

In March, @Aptos tokenholders voted to raise gas fees 10x and halve staking rewards. No new mechanism was needed as Aptos has burned every gas fee since launch. However, at the old prices that burn covered just 0.2% of issuance (now ~10%).

The repricing moved both sides at once. The burn went up while validator commission roughly halved along with issuance, and Token Holder Net Income went from around -ve $130K a week in January to positive by May.

Demand held as well. Daily transactions doubled to ~9M even at 10x the old fees, which is why the network now burns more in gas fees than it pays its operators.

text:
用什么来替代互联网的旧商业模式？这是未来五年最有意思的问题，Matthew Prince 在 Cloudflare Connect 2026 开幕 Keynote 给出了他们的答案：“先降负载，再给剩下的部分定价” 👀 

在今年五月，Cloudflare 检测到的 Agent 流量已超过人类流量，按现在的趋势外推，五年后 Agent 流量会是人类流量的 1000 倍，人类在网络上会变成“舍入误差”。原因不是人类不再上网，我们的流量大体持平，而是越来越多的内容由 Agent 来替人去消费。

Agent 替你跑腿，但跑腿是有成本的，谁来支付这些成本？Matthew 举了“中午去哪吃饭”的例子。Agent 会去翻上千家餐厅的菜单，最后只有一家拿到生意，其余 999 家都承担了被抓取的带宽和资源成本，这是一个典型的公地悲剧。去年他关注的是新闻出版商流量断崖式下跌，Cloudflare 为此和全球最大的一批出版商合作，向 AI 公司争取补偿。

今年他更担心的是街角的熟食店和餐馆这类小商家。人类光顾小店，是因为老板记得你的名字，或者店就在回家路上，这些情感和便利的因素对 Agent 完全不起作用。Agent 时间几乎无限，也不被情绪左右，它会选信息最多的那一家，也就是最大的公司。如果不加干预，市场会走向集中，新进入者和小企业越来越难生存。

Matthew 对此给了两个具体抓手：

第一是“只抓取变化的内容”。Google 式的抓取不管页面变没变都会重抓，AI 公司照搬了这种做法，非常低效。Cloudflare 与 OpenAI 合作，主动告诉对方哪些页面更新了，从而降低整个生态的总负载，连 Google 也认同这个方向。

第二是“代理使用你的内容时，你要能收到钱”。他把这两点概括成一句话：先降负载，再给剩下的部分定价。最后他强调 Cloudflare 做不到独自完成这件事，需要伙伴一起定义这个可持续的未来。

如果这个设想成立，那么 Agent Payment 就是这个新商业模式中最重要的一环；另外，不同系统的 Agent 之间要能主动通讯和全局协调，降低无效查询负载，我们会有非常多的面向 Agent Infra 的新系统需要建设🤔

A Labour Councillor has been given a 12-month suspended sentence for possessing indecent images of children deemed category A considered the worst.

Tom Dewey a Labour Councillor for Hackney has avoided jail after admitting possessing indecent images of children.

Recorder Jonathan Ashley-Norman handed down a 12-month suspended sentence, he said: Your actions have had a devastating impact on your life and your closest family.”

He gave him credit for an early guilty plea
He also ordered devices to be forfeited, told Dewey to pay £500 costs and put him on a 10-year Sexual Harm Prevention Order, which will restrict his contact with children.

Thomas Dewey, who was elected as a Labour councillor for De Beauvoir ward, was arrested by detectives from the National Crime Agency who seized laptops and tablets at his home in Hertford Road in Hackney, just days before May’s local elections last year.

He had a “huge problem” with looking at indecent images of children from the internet for his own use, Wood Green Crown Court heard.

Described by party activists as “ambitious”, he had worked at Hackney Council for nearly two years as a support officer for the Mayor and Cabinet office and for a consultancy advising on planning.

He was the branch secretary for the De Beauvoir ward for Labour and had spent years campaigning for the party in Hackney.

Last month, the 36-year-old admitted a charge of making five category A indecent images of children, a further charge of making 41 category B indecent images, as well as making 203 category C indecent images of children. 

Images are graded with category A considered the worst.

Dewey, now of Hampshire, also admitted a charge of possessing 78 extreme pornographic images of children – an act which results, or is likely to result, in serious injury to a person  and having 1,523 prohibited images of children in his possession.

The maximum sentence for the most serious charge is five years, depending on the number of images.

Details of the images were not read out in court, but prosecutor Margia Mostafa said the content of the Category A images “are highly serious.”

The starting point for the first charge is two years in prison but the steps Dewey has taken, along with his early guilty plea and remorse saw that cut to 12 months, suspended for two years.

He received an additional six months for charge two, three months for charge three, six months for charge four, and six months for charge five, all suspended for two years and to run concurrently.

Dewey also has to do 150 hours’ community service and 40 days of a “rehabilitation activity”.

Dewey was elected as a Labour councillor for the first time in the May 2022 council elections and resigned days later, triggering a by-election last July.

text:
让孙宇晨变严肃的人，33 岁测出 18 岁身体

一口气在水下游 319 米，憋气 9 分 08 秒，33 岁测出生理年龄 18 岁。
这是金明，圈内叫他仙道，就是前阵子和孙宇晨那期 47 分钟对谈里，让孙宇晨收起嬉皮笑脸、认真输出的主持人。

他的履历第一眼看像编的：
- 自由潜水国家队，中国第一位自由潜水世界纪录保持者，2025 年 11 月把纪录推到 319 米
- 哈佛读数学和计算机，学生时代就开始创业
- 极链科技创始人，27 岁拿到包括阿里在内的 10 亿元融资
- 湖畔大学四期最年轻的创一代学员
- 2010 年就开始拿特斯拉
- 前几天在 Token2049 的 Coinbase 全球交易赛拿了第三、亚洲第一

18 岁这个数字，是今年世锦赛后的尿检和身体检测结果。

那页 PPT 的标题叫「Bodily Time」，底下列了 A 到 O 一共 15 条，副标题是「针对普通人简化维持身体机能的建议」。
我按一天的顺序重新排了一遍，每条写清怎么做、花多少钱、为什么。

白天，先把生物钟对准

1. 每天晒太阳 10 分钟。
- 怎么做：白天出门，让自然光照到身上，每天固定做。
- 为什么：规律的自然光帮身体校准昼夜节律，晚上才困得准时。

晚上，把卧室变成只用来睡觉的地方

2. 卧室全暗，全年保持 21～24℃。
- 怎么做：关灯后检查窗帘四个角有没有漏光；温度定一个适合自己的数，一年四季不变。金明自己常年 24℃，所以一年到头盖同一套被子，不再分冬被夏被。
- 为什么：光线和温度稳定，身体每晚进入睡眠的条件就一样。

3. 床只用来睡觉。
- 怎么做：不在床上工作、刷手机、看视频，清醒时的事尽量搬到卧室外面。
- 为什么：让身体形成条件反射，一上床就知道该睡了。

4. 睡前站一会儿，再直接上床。
- 怎么做：睡前站着或走动 5 分钟，然后直接躺下睡。
- 为什么：体位一变，血液重新分布，帮人更快睡着。

5. 睡前用筋膜枪轻按后脑勺下方。
- 怎么做：用筋膜枪低档轻轻按枕下区，也就是后脑勺和脖子交界那一圈，3 分钟。
- 为什么：能缩短入睡时间。
- 实操提醒：PPT 上写的是「轻度」，颈部用筋膜枪有一定安全风险，力度宁轻勿重。

6. 换一张会控温的床套。
- 怎么做：Eight Sleep 智能床套铺在床垫上，整夜主动调节床面温度。
- 花多少：参考价 19999 到 37999 元。
- 为什么：金明说他用了快 10 个月，深睡时间多了约 21%，夜里醒来的次数也少了。

吃的，只有两条

7. 每天 3～5 克肌酸。
- 怎么做：金明的建议是女性 3 克、男性 5 克，中老年人和不练运动的人也可以考虑。
- 花多少：参考价 500 克 70 到 130 元，摊下来每月 13 到 39 元。
- 为什么：肌酸配合力量训练，对维持肌肉力量有帮助。

8. Omega-3、维生素 D，再加上运动。
- 怎么做：三样一起做。PPT 没写剂量；他引用的那项研究里，用的是每天 1 克 Omega-3、每天 2000 IU 维生素 D、每周 3 次每次 30 分钟的居家运动。
- 花多少：鱼油参考价每月 21 到 60 元，维生素 D3 每月 4 到 20 元。
- 为什么：三样结合能减少炎症、延缓衰老。这条我去翻了原论文，放到后面单独说。

测数据，知道自己在变好还是变差

9. 戴 Oura 戒指，运动时加一条 Polar 心率带。
- 怎么做：Oura 长期戴着看睡眠、心率、HRV（心率变异性，越高通常说明身体恢复得越好）。金明说坚持戴 3 到 6 个月，对自己身体的理解会明显提升；大部分人只戴 Oura 就够了。
- 花多少：Oura 4 参考价约 2350 元起，Oura 5 约 2680 元起，会员每月约 40 元；Polar H9 约 590 元，H10 500 到 900 元。
- 为什么：先看见数据，后面每一条改动才知道有没有用。

10. 定期测生物年龄。
- 怎么做：抽血做 DNA 甲基化检测，金明看三个指标：
PhenoAge：用生理指标或 DNA 甲基化估算你的身体是几岁
GrimAge：从 DNA 甲基化特征看和衰老相关的死亡风险
DunedinPACE：衰老速度，1 是平均速度，大于 1 老得快，小于 1 老得慢
- 花多少：参考价每次 1890 到 3680 元。
- 为什么：日历上的年龄每个人都一样，身体的年龄才是能改的那个数。

恢复，给身体做保养

11. 冷水洗脸，敷补水面膜。
- 怎么做：用冷水洗脸、敷面膜，重点是额头、鼻子这片 T 区。
- 为什么：人天生有潜水反射，冷水碰到脸，心率会慢下来；他认为这样能调节自律神经，提高 HRV、降低皮质醇（压力激素）。

12. 定期进高压氧舱。
- 怎么做：去民用微高压氧舱，按次付费。
- 花多少：参考价每小时 200 到 400 元。
- 为什么：它能帮肌肉组织恢复、缓解炎症；另一个好处是舱里不能带电子设备，顺便做了一次数字戒断。

心态，给大脑留白

13. 游戏，他还没想清楚。
- 金明说游戏的好处是练决策、练资源分配和效率优化；坏处是让大脑一直兴奋，影响休息。
- 他担心游戏对前额叶和脑电活动的影响，但认为还要继续研究。

14. 自己做点家务，学会浪费时间。
- 不是所有时间都要拿来工作、学习、提高效率，留一点给不为产出的事。

15. 普通人的体能上限，比自己以为的高。
